Topic 01 — Speed & Agility Mechanics

Three Related, Distinct Qualities

Speed
Ability to accelerate and reach maximal velocity.
Linear speed — sprinting.
COD Ability
Physical capacity to decelerate, change direction, and reaccelerate.
Purely physical — no reaction required.
Agility
COD ability + perceptual-cognitive ability.
Change of direction in response to a stimulus — perception-action coupling.
Acceleration matters for all three. What separates them: deceleration ability, movement mode, and reacting to a stimulus.

Topic 01 — Speed & Agility Mechanics
Physics of Sprinting, Change of Direction, and Agility
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Force
Rate of force development · Force & motion
  • To execute movement techniques, athletes must apply force — the product of mass and acceleration.
  • Force is the interaction of two physical objects: a push or pull exerted on one object by another, which prevents both from occupying the same space.
  • Force is a vector quantity: it has magnitude (size) and direction.
  • This movement of mass changes an object's velocity, causing acceleration.
2Speed vs velocity
Rate of force development · Force & motion
  • In strength and conditioning, speed and velocity are often used interchangeably — for sprint and agility performance they must be separated.
  • Speed is a scalar quantity: how fast an object is moving, i.e., the rate at which it covers a distance.
  • Velocity is a vector quantity: how fast an object travels and in what direction. Velocity is speed with a direction.
3Acceleration
Rate of force development · Force & motion
  • Acceleration is the rate at which an object's velocity changes over time.
  • Once a force acts on an object, the mass changes direction and leaves the space it occupied; acceleration continues if external forces continue to change velocity.
  • In practice, deceleration replaces "negative acceleration" for a change from higher to lower velocity.
4Two variables describe force over time
Rate of force development · Force & motion
  • Time available to produce force is limited in most athletic activities.
  • So two variables describe force relative to the time available: rate of force development (RFD) and impulse.
1Definition
Rate of force development · RFD
  • The development of maximal force in minimal time, typically used as an indicator of explosive strength.
  • RFD = change in force ÷ change in time.
2Rapid beats maximal force
Rate of force development · RFD
  • In sport, producing force rapidly is arguably more desirable than producing maximal force, given the time constraints of most high-intensity actions.
3Time available
Rate of force development · RFD
  • High maximal force improves jump height and other athletic measures, but most competitive scenarios don't allow time to generate it.
  • Maximal contraction force takes at least 300 ms; many sport activities use 0–200 ms.
4RFD as a measure
Rate of force development · RFD
  • Where success depends on timing of movement, RFD is a more useful measure of an athlete's impulsive ability.
5Rate and direction of force
Rate of force development · RFD
  • Accelerating a mass depends on a change in velocity from an external force.
  • To achieve higher acceleration, apply forces at a greater rate and orient force in the optimal direction.
1Force takes time
Impulse · Impulse
  • To change position, forces must be applied (to overcome inertia) to produce a change in velocity.
  • Athletes never apply force instantaneously when increasing locomotor speed.
2Stance and plant phases
Impulse · Impulse
  • Force is applied to the running surface over a period of time (impulse) in the stance phase of sprinting or the plant phase of changing direction.
  • The length of time in the stance or plant phase is the ground contact time.
3Impulse defined
Impulse · Impulse
  • Impulse = the force applied × the time it is applied. It is shown as the area under a force–time curve.
  • Changes in impulse change the athlete's momentum, and so the ability to accelerate or decelerate — underpinning human locomotion.
4Impulse–momentum relationship
Impulse · Impulse
  • Net impulse dictates the magnitude of the change of momentum.
  • Because mass remains constant in most sporting scenarios, increases in net impulse are proportionate to changes in velocity.
5Braking and propulsive phases
Impulse · Impulse
  • Vertical and horizontal forces differ in magnitude between the acceleration phase and the maximal-velocity phase (two different body positions).
  • Impulse is the area under the force–time curve in the braking phase (negative horizontal force) or the propulsive phase (positive horizontal force).
6Max velocity vs acceleration
Impulse · Impulse
  • In maximal-velocity phases, force production is asymmetrical and RFD is very high.
  • This gives much shorter ground contact times than in the acceleration phase.
1Momentum
Impulse · Momentum
  • Momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity.
  • During a sprint, an athlete's body mass remains constant.
2Greater impulse needs greater net force
Impulse · Momentum
  • Given the same time frame, the only way to achieve a greater impulse is to generate greater net force.
3Accelerate or decelerate
Impulse · Momentum
  • Greater net impulse increases or decreases momentum, depending on whether the athlete intends to accelerate or reaccelerate, or to decelerate before a COD or as an isolated action.
  • A change in impulse changes momentum, and is the cause of an object's movement.
4Train impulse as well as RFD
Impulse · Momentum
  • Within an individual step, the magnitude of the force and the length of time it is produced are paramount.
  • Training should focus on developing impulse (the area under the force–time curve) in addition to RFD.
1Why power isn't used here
Impulse · Power
  • Power is derived from force and velocity, so it is considered a mechanical construct.
2Measure what determines power
Impulse · Power
  • It can be more useful to directly measure the characteristics that determine power (force and velocity).
  • Measuring power alone doesn't give fully useful insight to practitioners.
3Force, RFD and impulse
Impulse · Power
  • Force, RFD and impulse are the direct, underlying characteristics that dictate explosive performance.
  • No more complex derived value is needed for additional insight.
1Overcome gravity
Practical implications for speed
  • To displace body mass down a track or field, athletes must produce forces sufficient to overcome gravity and create a positive change in velocity.
2Force to reach top speed
Practical implications for speed
  • Within a short sprint, force is the effort needed to accelerate the athlete up to his or her highest achievable speed.
  • That speed is largely determined by physiological factors.
3Shorter than maximal-force time
Practical implications for speed
  • These forces are produced rapidly, with time constraints shorter than the time needed for maximal voluntary force production.
  • So rate of force production may be a more important factor for sprinting success.
4Impulse matters too
Practical implications for speed
  • Since sprinting success depends largely on producing forces within a short amount of time, impulse is an important underlying factor.
1Braking impulse
Practical implications for COD and agility
  • In addition to acceleration, the production of braking forces over certain periods of time (foot contacts) — braking impulse — should be considered during COD, deceleration and agility maneuvers.
2Impulse reflects physical demand
Practical implications for COD and agility
  • The impulse required to change momentum effectively and efficiently is a direct reflection of the physical requirements for COD.
3Angle and entry velocity
Practical implications for COD and agility
  • As the required angle of directional change or the entry velocity into the COD increases, so does the impulse required to change momentum and deflect the center of mass.
  • So it is physically more demanding.
4Perceptual-cognitive time limits
Practical implications for COD and agility
  • Time restraints from the perceptual-cognitive aspects of agility can limit the time available to produce the required force (and impulse) to change direction in response to a stimulus.
5Speed vs agility
Practical implications for COD and agility
  • Speed requires the ability to accelerate and reach maximal velocity.
  • Agility requires perceptual-cognitive ability combined with the ability to decelerate, change direction, and reaccelerate in an intended direction.

Topic 02 — Neurophysiological Basis
Neurophysiological Basis for Speed
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Neuromuscular function
Nervous system
  • Vital to sprint performance: the activity and interaction of the central nervous system with the muscles influence the rate and strength of muscle contraction.
2Combined training adaptations
Nervous system
  • Strength, plyometric and sprint training together produce several neuromuscular adaptations that may contribute to improved sprint performance.
3Resistance training and neural drive
Nervous system
  • Resistance training enhances neural drive: the rate and amplitude of impulses sent from the nervous system to the target muscles.
4Neural drive → force
Nervous system
  • Increases in neural drive (a higher rate of action potentials) are related to increases in both muscular force production and the rate of force production.
5Plyometric training
Nervous system
  • Increases the excitability of high-threshold motor neurons.
  • Increased excitability ultimately enhances neural drive to the muscle.
6Result: RFD and impulse
Nervous system
  • Taken together, increases in neural drive may contribute to increases in the athlete's RFD and impulse generation.
1What the SSC is
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • Many functional tasks begin with preparatory countermovements involving spring-like actions: the SSC.
  • An eccentric–concentric coupling phenomenon: muscle–tendon complexes are rapidly and forcibly lengthened (stretch loaded), then immediately shortened in a reactive or elastic manner → enhanced concentric force production.
2Where it shows up
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • Seen in movements with a rapid transition from an eccentric to a concentric action.
  • Particularly prevalent in sports involving running, jumping, directional changes, and other explosive changes in velocity.
3Reactive strength
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • Reactive strength development is a highly important quality to develop in training programs.
  • It can be a distinct capability, independent of maximal strength in elite athletes.
4Reflex mechanisms
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • SSC actions exploit intrinsic muscle–tendon behavior as well as the force and length reflex feedback to the nervous system.
5Acute vs chronic effects
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • Acutely: tends to increase mechanical efficiency and impulse via elastic energy recovery.
  • Chronically: upregulates muscle stiffness and enhances neuromuscular activation.
6SSC training criterion 1
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • Skillful, multijoint movements that transmit forces through the kinetic chain and exploit elastic–reflexive mechanisms.
7SSC training criterion 2
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • To manage fatigue and emphasize work quality and technique, structure training around brief work bouts or clusters separated by frequent rest pauses.
8Complex or contrast training
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
  • A combination of progressive plyometric and heavy resistance methods can accomplish both objectives.
1Preactivation and muscle spindles
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • Strength and speed training may be linked to a rise in preactivation of the musculature used in sprinting.
  • The onset of pre-tension may relate to increased sensitivity of muscle spindles.
2Stiffness and tendon compliance
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • Better timing of feedback from muscle spindles → greater muscle stiffness and tendon compliance.
  • This supports the SSC, which underpins the SMM.
3The model
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • A mathematical model depicting sprinting as locomotion in which body-mass displacement is the aftereffect of energy produced and delivered through the coiling and extension of spring-like actions within muscle architecture.
  • In a running cycle, one spring compresses and propels the sprinter forward while the other swings forward for ground contact.
4Foot strike
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • Compression of the spring begins at foot strike, producing horizontal braking forces.
  • This sudden, brief deceleration assists in propelling the swing leg forward for the next step.
5Midstance
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • The center of mass moves ahead of the foot.
  • The spring is compressed to its lowest point, coinciding with a lowered center of mass.
6Push-off
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • The coiled spring extends, returning energy and force that project the sprinter forward.
7Elite sprinters deviate from the SMM
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • The SMM gives a conceptual framework for upright high-speed running, but recent investigations suggest its ability to describe the stance phase of elite sprinters is limited.
  • At max velocity, elite sprinters deviate from the classic SMM, producing much of their vertical force in the first half of ground contact.
8Non-elite sprinters fit the SMM
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • Most non-elite sprinters (e.g., team or field-based sports) show stance phases described by the SMM.
  • Their vertical force curve is more symmetrical.
9How to use the SMM
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • Use it to describe the relationship between the SSC, muscle stiffness and sprinting.
  • As stride frequency increases at a given running speed, a key feature of the leg spring is increased muscle stiffness.
10Training takeaway
Spring-mass model (SMM)
  • Because sprinting requires high speeds, prescribe exercises shown to increase neural drive while overloading the musculature of the hip, knee and ankle involved in the SSC.
1Contact times by action
COD and agility · Ground contact time
  • Plant-phase contact time in agility (0.23–0.25 s) or COD (~0.15–0.6 s, depending on angle) exceeds both sprint phases.
  • Sprint acceleration: 0.17–0.2 s. Maximal-velocity sprinting: 0.09–0.11 s.
2Bigger angle, longer contact
COD and agility · Ground contact time
  • As the intended angle of direction change (center-of-mass deflection) increases, ground contact time on the main plant foot typically increases.
  • Why: greater braking force, negative work (knee flexion) and deceleration demands with sharper changes.
3Braking then propulsive impulse
COD and agility · Ground contact time
  • The longer contact increases braking impulse to reduce momentum in the original direction.
  • A propulsive impulse then enables acceleration toward the new direction of travel.
4Fast vs slow SSC
COD and agility · Ground contact time
  • COD actions <45° can generally be considered fast SSC activities.
  • Direction changes >45° are generally slower SSC activities — depending on entry velocity and the athlete's physical capacity.
1Braking matters for agility
COD and agility · Eccentric training
  • Effective braking is an important part of agility performance.
  • So consider neuromuscular development with high-velocity, high-force eccentric muscle actions — for two reasons.
2Different recruitment
COD and agility · Eccentric training
  • First: the adaptations and motor unit recruitment pathways called on during an eccentric action differ from those in concentric contractions.
3Velocity-specific adaptations
COD and agility · Eccentric training
  • Second: adaptations to eccentric training appear to be specific to the velocity of eccentric loading.
1Beyond the physical
COD and agility · Perceptual-cognitive
  • Effective agility training requires knowledge of perceptual-cognitive demands over and above the neurophysiological requirements for changing direction.
2Perceptual-cognitive abilities
COD and agility · Perceptual-cognitive
  • Visual search scanning, anticipation, decision making, and reaction time.
3Tactical situation
COD and agility · Perceptual-cognitive
  • The tactical situation (offensive vs defensive) changes the brain processing strategy required.
4Putting it together
COD and agility · Perceptual-cognitive
  • Agility demands include: the SSC, eccentric muscle action neuromuscular training, and the time demand of the COD maneuver on the SMM.
  • They extend beyond physical requirements to perceptual-cognitive requirements specific to the tactical situation.
Additional neurophysiological considerations for COD and agility development.
Sprinting, agility and COD are all dynamic displays of force production in the athletic setting.

Topic 03 — Running Speed & Technique
Running Speed
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1What sprinting is
Sprinting basics
  • Sprinting is a series of coupled flight and support phases, known as strides.
  • It is orchestrated to displace the athlete's body down the track at maximal acceleration or velocity (or both), usually over brief distances and durations.
2Sprint duration
Sprinting basics
  • Sprinting has been described as rapid, unpaced, maximal-effort running of 15 seconds or less.
3Stride vs step
Sprinting basics
  • A stride is, e.g., right foot contact to the next right foot contact.
  • It is essentially made up of two steps: right to left, then left to right.
  • For clarity: one stride = two steps.
4Stance and flight phases
Sprinting basics
  • Stance: a braking period followed by a propulsive period.
  • Flight: the recovery and ground preparation (late swing) segments of the swing leg.
5Sprint phases
Sprinting basics
  • Linear sprinting is divided into the start, acceleration, and top speed.
  • All require the athlete to volitionally move the lower limbs at maximal speed through a series of stance and flight phases.
1The classic definition
Step length × step frequency
  • The classic definition of sprint speed concerns the relationship between step length and step frequency.
2Step length
Step length × step frequency
  • The distance between the toe and heel of two consecutive footsteps.
3Step frequency
Step length × step frequency
  • Also called rate: the number of steps per second.
4Two ways to go faster
Step length × step frequency
  • Sprint speed can be increased by an increase in step length or an increase in step frequency.
5The underlying factor
Step length × step frequency
  • These changes in performance variables are logical, but the underlying component to maximizing step length and step frequency is rapid force production.
1Force displaces mass
Elite vs novice sprinters · Step length
  • Application of force is needed to displace a mass.
  • In sprinting, step length represents the displacement of mass.
2Elite vs novice step length
Elite vs novice sprinters · Step length
  • Elite male sprinters achieve a step length of 2.70 m (8.9 ft).
  • Novice sprinters display a step length of 2.56 m (8.4 ft) at maximum velocity.
1More frequency, more force time
Elite vs novice sprinters · Step frequency
  • Contact with the ground is needed to continue force production and subsequent alterations in velocity.
  • So increasing step frequency theoretically maximizes the time available to produce force.
2Elite vs novice step frequency
Elite vs novice sprinters · Step frequency
  • Elite male sprinters: near 4.63 steps per second.
  • Novice sprinters: a lesser 4.43 steps per second.
1The single component
Elite vs novice sprinters · Force and contact time
  • The differences between elite and novice sprinters can be traced to a single component.
  • Much of the literature suggests that the amount of vertical force applied to the ground during the stance phase at top speed may be the most critical component to improving top speed.
2Shortest period possible
Elite vs novice sprinters · Force and contact time
  • These greater forces must be applied to the ground in the shortest period possible.
3Less contact time, bigger impulses
Elite vs novice sprinters · Force and contact time
  • Elite sprinters need less ground contact time with each step to exert the effort needed to displace their mass.
  • This is due to their ability to create greater impulses.
4More time in the air
Elite vs novice sprinters · Force and contact time
  • These faster sprinters also spend more time in the air.
1Similar swing-leg time
Elite vs novice sprinters · Knee height
  • Elite sprinters' times to reposition the swing leg are similar to those of their slower counterparts.
  • The time required for staging the next ground contact is also similar.
2Farther down the track
Elite vs novice sprinters · Knee height
  • Elite sprinters propel themselves farther down the track, due to properly directed vertical forces.
3Optimized knee height
Elite vs novice sprinters · Knee height
  • Mann suggests vertical forces are better directed toward the track due to an optimized knee height at maximal flexion of the recovering leg.
  • The higher knee position gives a greater time period for force production and subsequent ground clearance (range-of-motion force movement principle).
4Force in the first half of stance
Elite vs novice sprinters · Knee height
  • This technical advantage may be further evidence for why elite sprinters produce most of their force within the first half of the stance phase.
1Continuous high force
Elite vs novice sprinters · Top speeds
  • Faster sprinters reach higher velocities through continuous application of high forces in a short stance phase.
  • This results in longer steps, or steps occurring at a higher rate.
2Elite setting
Elite vs novice sprinters · Top speeds
  • In the elite setting (e.g., 100 m world championship finalists), male sprinters achieve velocities between 11.0 and 12.5 m/s (24.6–28.0 mph).
3Team sport athletes
Elite vs novice sprinters · Top speeds
  • Team sport athletes generally achieve maximum velocities of approximately 8.0 to 9.5 m/s (17.9–21.3 mph).
1Force production
What limits sprint speed
  • Force production is arguably the limiting factor.
2Technique and training
What limits sprint speed
  • Technical efficiency and properly designed training also limit sprint speed.
3Sprint speed summary
What limits sprint speed
  • Sprint speed is determined by an athlete's step length and step frequency.
  • More successful sprinters tend to have longer step lengths, as a result of properly directed forces into the ground, while also demonstrating a more frequent step rate.
4Two primary limiting factors
What limits sprint speed
  • These findings suggest that RFD and proper biomechanics are two of the primary limiting factors influencing sprint performance.

Topic 03 — Running Speed & Technique
Sprint Technique Checklist
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Set position
Start checklist
  • Distribute balanced body weight through the set position (blocks, or a three- or four-point staggered start).
  • Use the segment angles that are critical for producing explosive force from the start.
  • Front lower-leg angle ≈ 90°; rear lower-leg angle ≈ 120–135°.
2Front-leg drive
Start checklist
  • Aggressive extension of the hip, knee and ankle of the front leg against the block or ground.
3Rear-leg recovery
Start checklist
  • After initially extending at the hip and knee, the rear leg rapidly flexes.
  • Hip to ~90°, knee to ~90°, ankle to neutral — in preparation for foot contact of the first step.
4Arms
Start checklist
  • As the rear leg drives forward, the opposite arm drives forward too.
  • It mirrors the range of motion and timing of the rear leg.
  • Range of motion at each shoulder is large.
5Head
Start checklist
  • Neutral, looking a few yards or meters ahead along the track.
1Forward lean
Acceleration · Posture
  • Forward inclination helps maximize propulsive force contribution and depends on the absolute magnitude of force available.
  • The forward lean gradually reduces with each step, reaching an upright position by maximum velocity.
2Neutral pelvis
Acceleration · Posture
  • The pelvis position should be neutral relative to the torso.
3Center of mass ahead of the foot
Acceleration · Posture
  • The center of mass should be ahead of the foot during early acceleration (first few steps).
  • It gradually progresses to slightly behind the foot as the athlete progresses to maximum velocity.
4Low start, rising COM and hips
Acceleration · Posture
  • The center of mass and hip position begin low and rise higher with each step, from early to late acceleration to maximum velocity.
1Wide arm range of motion
Acceleration · Arm action
  • The ranges of motion in the arms are wide, to match the ranges of motion in the lower body on the contralateral side.
  • E.g., as the knee travels forward, the opposite arm travels forward.
2Aggressive backward drive
Acceleration · Arm action
  • The arms are driven aggressively backward.
1Longer steps, shorter contacts
Acceleration · Leg action
  • Each step gets progressively longer.
  • Ground contact times get shorter and flight times longer as the athlete advances to maximum velocity.
2Thigh split
Acceleration · Leg action
  • Rapid, large split of the thighs through the stance phase enhances leg extension force.
  • It also prepares the swing limb for rapid acceleration back down to the ground, enabling high ground reaction forces (GRF) early during ground contact.
3Low heel recovery
Acceleration · Leg action
  • Low heel recovery enables shorter steps and more cycle time dedicated to force production.
  • Heel recovery gains more height as the athlete progresses to maximum velocity.
4Piston-like foot path
Acceleration · Leg action
  • The path of the heel and rest of the foot tends to be piston-like (backward and downward).
  • It progresses to a more cyclic action by maximum velocity.
5Shin angles
Acceleration · Leg action
  • Forward-oriented shin angles gradually become more vertical as the athlete progresses to maximum velocity.
6Back-side catch
Acceleration · Leg action
  • Rapid deceleration of the extending thigh (back-side catch) during late stance avoids prolonging ground contact.
  • It then enables rapid subsequent recovery of the leg after takeoff.
7Late-swing thigh retraction
Acceleration · Leg action
  • The thigh forcefully retracts during late swing to enable foot contact behind the center of mass.
  • This enhances production and direction (more horizontal) of GRFs early in ground contact.
8Foot and ankle stiffness
Acceleration · Leg action
  • The foot and ankle maintain optimal stiffness.
  • A stable foot position during early stance provides the foundation for the hip extensors to contribute more effectively to forward propulsion, while enabling storage and release of elastic energy at the ankle.
1Slight forward lean
Maximum Velocity · Posture
  • The athlete maintains a slight forward lean.
2Neutral head
Maximum Velocity · Posture
  • Head in a neutral position, looking toward the intended direction of travel.
3High neutral pelvis
Maximum Velocity · Posture
  • High, neutral pelvis position.
1Arms mirror the legs
Maximum Velocity · Arm action
  • Arm action mirrors the contralateral limb.
  • When the touchdown leg is in its longest position, the opposite arm is in its most open position to balance the body.
2Hand path: waist to chin
Maximum Velocity · Arm action
  • The hand is driven hard down below the waist on the downstroke.
  • It returns to the height of the chin, with a more acute elbow angle (≈ 90° on the return).
3No midline crossing
Maximum Velocity · Arm action
  • Arms should not cross the midline of the body.
1Takeoff position
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • Slight knee flex at takeoff.
  • Hip hyperextended and ankle plantar flexed.
2Recovery after toe-off
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • After toe-off, the knee flexes and the ankle dorsiflexes (passive folding) as the thigh flexes forward at the hip to a high knee position.
  • High heel recovery: the foot steps over the opposite knee.
3Front-side catch
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • Knee at its highest point, with the tibia in a high, forward position.
  • This provides space for rearward acceleration of the thigh, helping generate larger initial GRFs during support.
4Down-and-back foot path
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • The foot travels down and back (negative foot speed before touchdown).
5Touchdown position
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • The foot touches down close to underneath the center of mass (slightly in front).
  • At touchdown, the opposite knee is beside or slightly in front of the knee of the touchdown leg.
6Minimal flexion in support
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • During support, knee and ankle flexion should be minimal.
7Back-side catch
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • In late stance, early hip flexor activation avoids prolonged ground contact and decelerates the extending limb.
  • This prevents lower-leg recovery behind the body after toe-off (too much back-side mechanics).
  • Result: better timing and an improved front-side position.
8Relaxation and rhythm
Maximum Velocity · Leg action
  • Rapid, efficient switching of limb positions requires efficient timing, enabled by rapid switching off of key muscles.
  • Relaxation and rhythm are essential for optimal timing and coordination, and for reducing energy demands.
Based on linear sprinting — use for instruction and evaluation. Adapted from Mann (2011).
Topic 03 — Running Speed & Technique
Technique Errors
Error
Error
1Hips are too high at the start of the crouch position.
CauseMisunderstanding of setup.
Coaching correction
  • Space the feet 1.5–2 foot lengths apart.
  • Lower into the starting position by dropping the back-leg shin parallel to the sprint surface.
2Stepping out laterally during the initial drive phase.
CauseImproper distribution of forces.
Coaching correction
  • Push or drive through the ground to initiate the sprint.
3Arm movement is abnormally short and tight.
CauseMisunderstanding of natural arm swing.
Coaching correction
  • Either (a) drive the elbow down and back, or (b) pull the hands down and back, as if pulling on a rope.
  • Let the hands fully break the waist.
  • Recover the arms at the midline of the body (invisible line from nose through navel).
4Holding unnecessary tension in the dorsal muscles and hyperextending the neck.
CauseMisunderstanding of movement.
Coaching correction
  • Keep the head in line with the spine.
  • Torso and head rise at the same rate during the acceleration and transition phases of the sprint.
5Jumping the first step, or stepping over the knee of the stance leg.
CausePush-off angle too high; upward thrust too steep.
Coaching correction
  • Initiate movement by driving through the ground.
  • Let the swing leg cut horizontally across the stance-leg shin (ankle crossover), not step over the stance leg (knee crossover).
  • Keep the swing-leg foot close to the ground to set up a proper acceleration phase.
6Getting into an upright posture prematurely.
CauseInadequate push-off force; improper carriage of the head.
Coaching correction
  • Keep pushing into the ground while maintaining a natural trunk lean.
  • Keep the head in line with the spine. Lifting the head may suddenly lift the torso and minimize acceleration patterns.
1Superficially trying to maintain an acceleration phase when the shins are clearly vertical.
CauseImproper understanding of movement patterns.
Coaching correction
  • As the shins and hips come up to vertical, so should the torso and head.
  • Feel for the rise in the hips so the joints (shoulders → hips → ankles) stay stacked or in line.
  • This position allows proper transmission of forces into the running surface.
2Not displaying optimal front-side mechanics (swing-leg knee height).
CauseInadequate force production and hip mobility.
Coaching correction
  • Swing-leg knee height (traditionally front-side mechanics) is influenced by GRFs and hip mobility.
  • Cueing the athlete to "lift the knees" may further disrupt force transmission and change the musculature naturally used in the sprint.
3Overstriding.
CauseMisunderstanding of force application.
Coaching correction
  • Sprint success comes from producing high vertical forces in a short time.
  • Overstriding tries to gain speed through larger ground contact times → dampens the SSC and lowers step frequency.
  • Instruct athletes to run in their lane and maintain their natural gait cycle.
4Chronic hamstring injury or pain.
CauseInsufficient mobility; improper positioning of the pelvis.
Coaching correction
  • High injury likelihood in the swing phase, due to eccentric (lengthening) forces or overstriding.
  • Anterior pelvic tilt compounds the risk.
  • Reduce anterior pelvic tilt by developing back-side and front-side mechanics through sprint drills.*
5Cycling the leg action: longer swing phase, with an open gap between the knees during stance.
CauseImproper force application.
Coaching correction
  • Drive the foot down and back into the track — do not paw.
  • Coaches often miscue "paw" because the foot seems to move horizontally in a sprint.
  • Pawing horizontally prevents use of vertical forces and overloads the SSC to move down the track.
  • Integrate appropriate sprint drills* to develop the correct leg action.
6Erratic arm movement in the transverse plane.
CauseImproper understanding of movement pattern.
Coaching correction
  • Often blamed on fatigue, but much literature suggests speed is limited by mechanical force application, not metabolic efficiency.
  • Drive the arms down and back while keeping an upright torso.
  • Recover the arm swing near the midline of the body to use the glenohumeral joint's natural range of motion.
*See sprint drills 1–6 (Topic 09: Speed & Agility Drills).
Topic 04

Methods of
Developing
Speed

Maximal-velocity phase: much shorter ground contact
Step length–frequency interaction as a function of running velocity (4–10 m/s)
Topic 04 — Primary, Secondary & Tertiary Methods
Methods of Developing Speed
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Max-velocity sprinting comes first
Primary · Max-velocity sprinting
  • Many training stimuli help optimize athletic performance.
  • But no exercise improves running velocity more than maximum-velocity sprinting.
2High force in short time
Primary · Max-velocity sprinting
  • An athlete's sprint prowess depends on generating high forces in short time periods.
3RFD and impulse
Primary · Max-velocity sprinting
  • Neurological adaptations from long-term plans that emphasize maximal strength and movement velocity improve both RFD and impulse generation.
4Upright sprinting is plyometric
Primary · Max-velocity sprinting
  • Upright sprinting uses the SSC, which defines it as a plyometric movement.
  • Chronic exposure to SSC movements can increase muscle stiffness — a potential physiological advantage for sprint ability.
5Near-maximal muscle activation
Primary · Max-velocity sprinting
  • Sprinting requires near-maximum to maximum muscle activation, which depends on high central nervous system activity.
  • Chronic exposure may therefore improve musculoskeletal control via the CNS.
6Cyclical dose–response
Primary · Max-velocity sprinting
  • Neurophysiological adaptations from previous practices bolster subsequent training.
1Resisted and assisted sprint training
Secondary · Resisted and assisted sprint training
  • Secondary methods: used to either enhance the force required or target potential neuromuscular adaptations for sprinting improvement.
  • Resisted sprinting and assisted sprinting.
2Benefits, drawbacks, coaching
Secondary · Resisted and assisted sprint training
  • Outlined on the Assisted vs Resisted slide.
1Weightlifting and jump training
Tertiary · Strength training
  • Prescribed to develop RFD and impulse at varying loads, because these movements use the SSC (tertiary methods).
2Large forces in brief time
Tertiary · Strength training
  • Sprint speed is underpinned by the ability to produce large forces within brief time periods.
  • Forces must be large enough to support body weight against gravity and displace the body through an increase in velocity.
3Weight room to track or field
Tertiary · Strength training
  • Central question: how best to transfer newly developed strength qualities from the weight room to the track or field?
4Specificity of training
Tertiary · Strength training
  • Transfer may require emphasis on specificity: dynamic correspondence and coordinative overload.
  • It depends on similarities between an exercise and the sporting environment in movement patterns, peak force, RFD, acceleration and velocity patterns.
5Merge maximal strength and speed-strength
Tertiary · Strength training
  • Training for maximal strength may help, but training should emphasize agendas that merge maximal strength and speed-strength qualities.
6Exercise selection and adaptations
Tertiary · Strength training
  • Choose exercises that let athletes display forces and velocities like those in sprinting.
  • These may most benefit rate coding and firing frequency, and alterations to type II fibers (cross-sectional area, fascicle length).
7Weightlifting derivatives
Tertiary · Strength training
  • Clean, snatch and mid-thigh pulls may enhance sprint performance.
  • Adaptations: muscular stiffness, enhanced RFD, and coactivation of the musculature around the hips and knees.
1Mobility vs flexibility
Mobility
  • Mobility: the freedom of an athlete's limb to move through a desired range of motion.
  • Flexibility: a joint's total range of motion.
2Tools
Mobility
  • Soft tissue manipulation is commonly used with speed athletes, though it is not a kinetic variable.
  • Tools: stretching, chiropractic care, massage, myofascial release — to achieve optimal mobility within the dynamic state.
3Positional limits
Mobility
  • Positional characteristics are among several limiting factors in performance.
4Hip flexion and misplaced forces
Mobility
  • Insufficient hip flexion restricts thigh and knee lift in flight.
  • An athlete may have the physical characteristics for high rates of force, but compromised freedom of movement misplaces forces → dampened sprint speed and increased injury likelihood.
5Postural integrity first
Mobility
  • Ensure proper postural integrity is in place before the onset of practice or competition.
Maximal speed comes from well-organized programming that organically develops the required skills, with emphasis and de-emphasis of qualities such as acceleration and maximum velocity in each training phase, coordinated through phasic progression.
Topic 04 — Methods of Developing Speed
Assisted vs Resisted
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Exposure to higher velocities
Assisted · Benefits
  • Theoretically exposes the athlete to higher velocities than can be reached in unassisted sprinting.
  • It does this by inducing an increased step rate or stride length, and exposing the athlete to higher hip angular velocities.
2Neuromuscular adaptation
Assisted · Benefits
  • The increased step rate is hypothesized to drive neuromuscular adaptations that increase maximal sprint velocity.
  • Increases in overspeed should be limited to ≤10%.
1Rushed stance phase
Assisted · Drawbacks
  • May prematurely rush the stance phase, removing the time needed to exert optimal forces.
  • Shown to decrease muscle activation and propulsive force production compared with maximal running → chop steps may be seen.
  • Leaning back and overstriding may appear as a protective, suboptimal braking response.
2More braking with towing
Assisted · Drawbacks
  • Exercises that rely on towing may increase braking forces compared with maximal running.
  • Athletes are trying to tolerate velocities they cannot naturally create or accommodate, because of biomechanical efficiency, training state, or both.
3Downhill eccentric load and SSC
Assisted · Drawbacks
  • Downhill sprinting may expose the athlete to unnecessary eccentric forces through a modified stance leg (having to find the ground).
  • It may also affect the SSC, which is optimized by foot placement just in front of the center of mass at ground contact in flat-surface upright sprinting.
4Little research support
Assisted · Drawbacks
  • Very little research supports overspeed training to date.
  • Sprint success comes from producing large forces in a short ground contact time.
1Develop top speed with natural, safer tools
Assisted · Coaching
  • Top-speed sprinting should be developed through more natural and safer training tools.
  • Consider the athlete's training status and support optimal biomechanics.
2Assess first; best for advanced athletes
Assisted · Coaching
  • Carefully assess the implications of assistance modalities before implementation.
  • They may be best used with advanced or elite athletes.
1Acceleration mechanics
Resisted · Benefits
  • Accentuates the biomechanics of the acceleration phase.
  • Places the athlete in a position that promotes forward trunk lean and lowered hip and shin angles.
2Overloads the acceleration phase
Resisted · Benefits
  • May optimize the ability to cover short distances quickly by overloading the acceleration phase.
  • Results in ground contact times that produce higher propulsive forces.
3Better acceleration → higher top speed
Resisted · Benefits
  • Improving acceleration (a change in velocity) may increase top speed through enhanced RFD.
4Load by velocity decrement
Resisted · Benefits
  • Resisted sprints and loads can be set by velocity decrements.
  • They can be manipulated to target technical, speed-strength power, and strength-speed qualities.
5Sport specificity
Resisted · Benefits
  • May offer specificity when athletes need to push (move) external mass, such as in bobsled, rugby and American football.
1Load too heavy
Resisted · Drawbacks
  • A load that is too great may lead to longer ground contact times and shorter step lengths that are not task specific.
2Incline too steep
Resisted · Drawbacks
  • Slopes that are too great may modify proper sprinting biomechanics.
  • This rehearses improper technique and limits transfer of the training effect.
3Sled pushing alters the gait cycle
Resisted · Drawbacks
  • Sled pushing may alter the natural sprinting gait cycle.
  • It removes the arm action that synchronizes and counterbalances the leg action at the hip.
1Maintain normal mechanics
Resisted · Coaching
  • To improve the acceleration phase, consider modalities that maintain the normal biomechanics of unresisted sprints.
2Choose load by sport and athlete
Resisted · Coaching
  • Choose loads based on the sporting context and the athlete's physical status.
  • Track and field sprinters: loads that do not decrease running velocity by more than 10–12%.
3Field sport athletes
Resisted · Coaching
  • Athletes who overcome external resistance while blocking, tackling and scrimmaging can use loads of 20–30% of body weight, to improve the initial 5–10 m of movement.
  • Friction affects the resistance experienced → prescribe sled pushes and pulls by velocity decrement.
Example modalities: rope towing, bungee cord pulls, or downhill running — with the intention of letting the athlete run at supramaximal speeds (overspeed training).
Example modalities: sled towing, sled pushing, wind resistance, incline sprinting — with the intention of improving accelerative abilities.
Assistance and resistance training for speed development.

Topic 05 — Agility Performance & COD Ability
Agility Performance and Change-of-Direction Ability
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Preplanned COD
COD and agility
  • In both field and court sports, there is a substantial number of preplanned COD movements.
  • In baseball, softball, American football and basketball, athletes decide before starting to move which path they will run.
2Quick or sudden COD
COD and agility
  • Such patterns often include a quick or sudden COD.
  • Examples: exploding into a sprint out of a shuffle off a base, or running a route before receipt of a ball.
3Reactive COD
COD and agility
  • Many sports also include rapid COD in response to teammates, opponents or tactical situations (external stimuli).
  • Such responses can occur in an offensive or a defensive scenario.
4Different demands
COD and agility
  • The physical movement and the perceptual-cognitive aspects of such performances impose different demands on the athlete.
5COD ability + agility
COD and agility
  • Understand the factors behind agility performance from a physical standpoint (COD ability), in combination with the perceptual-cognitive aspects (agility).
6How athletes improve
COD and agility
  • Athletes improve COD ability through developing several physical factors and technical skills, across a variety of speeds and modes of movement.
  • Developing agility also requires improving perceptual-cognitive abilities in relation to the demands of the sport.
1Plant phase insight
Factors affecting COD
  • Ground contact time and GRF during the plant phase provide valuable insight into the physical factors that affect COD performance.
  • Perceptual-cognitive factors must also be considered for agility.
2Shallow cutting angles
Factors affecting COD
  • COD and agility movements at shallow cutting angles (<75°) have shorter ground contact times (<250 ms).
  • They benefit from training similar to speed training for the physical demands, but still need additional perceptual-cognitive training.
3Sharp cutting angles
Factors affecting COD
  • With a more aggressive cutting angle (≥75°), ground contact time can often exceed 250 ms because of the greater braking requirements.
4Training emphasis at sharp angles
Factors affecting COD
  • Consider increasing emphasis on eccentric strength for braking and maximal strength.
  • Pair it with the concentric impulsiveness required for propulsion during the reacceleration.
5Reactive strength
Factors affecting COD
  • Because of the eccentric–concentric coupling during the plant phase of directional changes, reactive strength development is also a key training priority.
6Angle and agility effects
Factors affecting COD
  • Various requirements (angle of COD, or the perceptual-cognitive requirement of agility) may affect the GRF and ground contact times of athletes.
7Method of changing direction
Factors affecting COD
  • Of particular interest: the effect of the method of changing direction (for the same angle) on GRF and ground contact times.
  • Example: the 5-0-5 performed with a single-leg COD (outside leg turn) or a jump turn — usable in testing but not commonly performed on the field of play.
8Technique dictates demands
Factors affecting COD
  • The technique chosen dictates the demands.
  • To elicit a specific adaptation from an athlete, give specific instructions.
1Test affects perceived ability
Testing COD and agility · Interpreting tests
  • The test used to assess agility affects the perceived agility ability of the athlete.
  • A plethora of tests are used to assess "agility."
2COD test vs agility test
Testing COD and agility · Interpreting tests
  • Tests without a reactive aspect should be considered COD tests.
  • A test that includes a reactive stimulus is, by definition, a test of agility for most sports.
3Be informed and critical
Testing COD and agility · Interpreting tests
  • The requirements of a test may result in assessment of factors other than COD ability or perceptual-cognitive requirements.
  • So be informed and critical about any test used to assess "agility" or "change-of-direction ability."
4Illinois test example
Testing COD and agility · Interpreting tests
  • If the Illinois agility test (often performed with soccer athletes) is used after preseason training, improvements may reflect improved metabolic capacity, not necessarily improved COD ability.
  • Its length imposes a higher metabolic demand than shorter tests, so it is more representative of maneuverability.
1Similar length, different tests
Testing COD and agility · Types of COD tests
  • Even similar-length tests — traditional 5-0-5, modified 5-0-5 (without the initial 10 m run-up) and the L-run — have only a moderate relationship in the same athletes.
  • They are not all assessing the same type of COD ability or the same physical requirements.
2Rapid vs multiple COD
Testing COD and agility · Types of COD tests
  • Some tests require a rapid COD, others multiple COD.
  • Multiple-COD tests often involve bending around an object or cone while maintaining as much velocity as possible; a sharp COD (e.g., 5-0-5) demands rapid deceleration.
3Maneuverability
Testing COD and agility · Types of COD tests
  • Tests such as the Illinois agility test or L-run, which require a bend to maintain velocity instead of an aggressive COD, can be considered tests of maneuverability.
1Reactive agility tests
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Tests: COD speed and perceptual-cognitive ability.
  • Metabolic requirement: <3 s.
25-0-5
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Tests: COD speed.
  • Metabolic requirement: <3 s.
35-10-5
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Tests: COD speed.
  • Metabolic requirement: <5 s.
4T-test
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Tests: COD speed and maneuverability.
  • Metabolic requirement: <12 s*.
5Illinois agility
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Tests: maneuverability.
  • Metabolic requirement: <12 s*.
6L-run
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Tests: maneuverability.
  • Metabolic requirement: <6 s.
7Z-drill
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Trains: COD speed and maneuverability.
  • Duration: <5 s†.
8Y-shaped agility drill (generic stimulus)
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Trains: COD speed.
  • Duration: <5 s†.
9Y-shaped agility drill (specific stimulus)
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • Trains: COD speed and perceptual-cognitive ability.
  • Duration: <5 s†.
10Notes
Testing COD and agility · Tests & drills
  • * The length of the test strongly influences the metabolic requirements, and whether changes in test performance reflect enhanced conditioning rather than improvements in COD or agility ability.
  • † Drill duration depends on the distances used in the drill's design; keep it short to emphasize technical execution.
1Choose different tests
Testing COD and agility · Choosing and isolating
  • An athlete's measured COD ability may vary with the demand imposed by the chosen test.
  • So choose different tests that measure COD ability under a high-velocity braking requirement, with multiple COD, or in reaction to a scenario, opponent or stimulus.
2Match the sport
Testing COD and agility · Choosing and isolating
  • Consider the aspect most important to the given sport when determining COD and agility abilities.
  • Test and monitor various types of COD ability, and the perceptual-cognitive abilities required during true agility tests.
3Linear speed influence
Testing COD and agility · Choosing and isolating
  • Tests such as the traditional 5-0-5 may be influenced by an athlete's linear running speed.
4COD deficit
Testing COD and agility · Choosing and isolating
  • To isolate COD ability, determine the COD deficit: 5-0-5 test time − 10 m linear sprint time.
5Sprint momentum
Testing COD and agility · Choosing and isolating
  • Sprint momentum = average velocity during a linear sprint test (or the 10 m approach of the 5-0-5) × the athlete's mass.
  • It indicates the braking demand experienced during the 5-0-5, giving a more complete view of COD ability.
1Decelerate → reorient → reaccelerate
COD ability · What determines COD
  • COD ability is determined by the combination of the ability to decelerate (high braking impulse), reorient the body to face or partially face the direction of travel, and reaccelerate (high propulsive impulse) over short contact times.
2Body orientation
COD ability · What determines COD
  • Consider the orientation of the body leading into the deceleration, through the transition phase as the athlete stops, and the positioning as he or she reaccelerates out of the COD.
  • So the positioning of the trunk influences COD performance.
3Physical capacity
COD ability · What determines COD
  • The athlete needs the physical capacity to produce high and rapid magnitudes of force, tolerate the high loads associated with braking, and adopt favorable postures for braking and propulsion.
4Functional mass
COD ability · What determines COD
  • Increased muscle mass combined with decreased body fat (improving functional mass) is a predictor of COD performance (T-test, elite basketball players).
5Anthropometrics
COD ability · What determines COD
  • Height and limb length are not modifiable by the strength and conditioning professional, so they are not discussed.
6Center of mass height
COD ability · What determines COD
  • Body center of mass height is related to improved lateral COD performance.
  • It can be actively targeted during technique modification training.
7What improves COD ability
COD ability · What determines COD
  • Across various angles, COD ability improves with: increased hip extension velocity (rapid force application by the hip extensors); low COM height; wide lateral foot plants for perpendicular force application; increased braking and propulsive impulse.
  • Also: increased knee flexion entering the COD; minimized trunk angular displacement entering the COD (deceleration phase); increased lateral trunk tilt (during 180° changes).
1Well-rounded strength
COD ability · Training braking and strength
  • Decelerating, holding position and reaccelerating are important, so a well-rounded approach to strength is needed: dynamic, isometric and in particular eccentric strength capacities.
  • Training methods should span the entire load–velocity and force–velocity curve, across multiple lower-limb and trunk segments.
2Train braking specifically
COD ability · Training braking and strength
  • In contrast to sprint development, athletes should train so the neuromuscular system adapts to the rate of loading required during the braking phase.
  • Braking capacity must be specifically trained using low- and high-velocity eccentric muscle actions.
3Eccentric examples
COD ability · Training braking and strength
  • Drop landings; landing from a loaded jump; the catch phase of a power clean or power snatch; supramaximal eccentrics that particularly load the knee extensors.
  • All place different eccentric loading demands on the hips, knees and ankles.
4Approach speed and COD angle
COD ability · Training braking and strength
  • The biomechanical demands of directional changes are influenced by approach speed and COD angle.
  • Manipulate these two variables cautiously when designing COD and agility activities.
1Physical ability first
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • When the physical ability to change direction rapidly is present, focus on developing the perceptual-cognitive components.
  • These bring together the ability to perform both physically and mentally on the field of play.
2Components
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • Visual scanning, anticipation, pattern recognition, knowledge of the situation, decision-making time and accuracy, and reaction time.
3Sport specific
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • Many of these aspects of development are sport specific; a comprehensive discussion is beyond the scope of this text.
  • General drills to improve these skills are covered in the section on methods of developing agility.
4Visual focus (coaching)
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • When changing direction in response to an opponent (offensive or defensive), visually scan the environment and opponent, focusing on the shoulders, trunk and hip.
  • Following the anticipation of the event (unless deception is intended), quickly redirect attention to a new area to help lead the transition of the body.

Topic 05 — Agility Performance & COD Ability
Transitional Movements Checklist
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Split stance
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Stand in a split stance, ensuring stability.
2Sink the hips
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Lower the center of mass by sinking the hips.
3Front hip and knee
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Flex the front hip and knee to approximately 45°.
4Back knee and hips
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Flex the back knee to approximately 90° and the hips to around 60°.
5Foot position and weight
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Front foot flat (firm base of support); rear foot heel raised.
  • Distribute weight toward the balls of both feet.
6Flat back
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Keep the back flat.
7Torso lean
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Lean the torso, with the shoulders over the front knee.
8Head up
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Head up, looking forward (or toward the opponent; visual scanning).
9Relaxed arms
Backpedal · Starting stance
  • Relax the arms and hang them straight ahead of the hips.
1Drive off the back leg
Backpedal · First step
  • To initiate movement, drive off the back leg by extending the back-leg knee and hip.
  • The center of mass (COM) moves behind the center of pressure at toe-off.
2Low heel recovery
Backpedal · First step
  • Using a low heel recovery, the front leg moves back behind the rear leg.
  • It makes the next ground contact underneath the hips.
3Toe-to-heel contact
Backpedal · First step
  • Each foot contact should be toe to heel (never heel first).
4Low hips
Backpedal · First step
  • Keep the hips low to increase stability.
5Forward trunk lean
Backpedal · First step
  • Maintain a forward trunk lean.
6Head up
Backpedal · First step
  • Keep the head up and looking forward (or toward an opponent).
7Arm movement
Backpedal · First step
  • Relaxed contralateral arm movement, matching the timing and amplitude of the leg movement.
  • Range of motion at the shoulder should be small.
8Foot alignment and step width
Backpedal · First step
  • Hips, knees and ankles aligned in the frontal plane.
  • Avoid planting the foot wider than the hips (maintains torso and pelvic position, i.e., hip step-width), and avoid a narrow step width.
1Rapid limb switching
Backpedal · Subsequent steps
  • With each step, use a low heel recovery to keep the feet close to the ground (rapid limb switching with minimal knee separation on ground contact).
  • This enables a quicker transition to a subsequent movement (e.g., COD or forward sprint).
2Low hips
Backpedal · Subsequent steps
  • Keep the hips low to maintain a low COM and quicken the transition into the next movement (minimize vertical oscillation).
  • Possible cues: "stay low" or "drop the hips."
3Toe-to-heel contact
Backpedal · Subsequent steps
  • Each foot contact should be toe to heel.
  • Possible cue: "toe to heel."
4Feet in line with hips
Backpedal · Subsequent steps
  • Ensure foot contact is in line with the hips in the frontal plane, to avoid feet crossing and the risk of trips or falls.
5Forward trunk lean
Backpedal · Subsequent steps
  • Maintain a forward trunk lean.
6Head up
Backpedal · Subsequent steps
  • Keep the head up and looking forward (or toward an opponent).
  • Possible cues: "eyes up" or "head up."
7Arm movement
Backpedal · Subsequent steps
  • Use a relaxed, low-amplitude contralateral arm movement.
  • Objective: project the COM rearward, with minimal vertical projection and oscillation.
1Athletic ready position
Side-shuffle · Start position
  • Feet shoulder-width apart; weight toward the balls of the feet.
  • Flex the hips, knees and ankles (strong quarter-squat position).
  • Back flat with a torso lean (shoulders over knees).
  • Head up; arms by the sides with elbows flexed and hands in front of the body.
1Balls of the feet
Side-shuffle · Foot position
  • Foot contact is on the balls of the feet.
2Feet perpendicular to movement
Side-shuffle · Foot position
  • Feet are placed perpendicular to movement (parallel, or slight hip external rotation).
3Close to the ground
Side-shuffle · Foot position
  • Feet stay close to the ground.
4Wide base
Side-shuffle · Foot position
  • Foot placement is wider than the knees.
  • Increased width increases stability and lowers the COM.
5No crossing
Side-shuffle · Foot position
  • The feet should not cross.
  • In a diagonal or faster shuffle, the feet may cross using a crossover step, to help with the directional change or provide extra propulsion to increase velocity.
1Short steps, drive from the far leg
Side-shuffle · Leg action
  • Take short steps, driving more from the leg farthest from the intended direction of travel (pushing the medial aspect of the foot).
  • The COM moves medially relative to the center of pressure at toe-off, with the other leg acting as a pivot.
  • This lets the COM travel medially and assists the shuffle step (COM is now over the center of pressure).
2Leg action close to the ground
Side-shuffle · Leg action
  • Leg action is close to the ground in preparation for ground contact.
1COM projection
Side-shuffle · COM travel
  • The COM is projected medially or laterally, with minimal vertical projection and oscillation.
2Loaded legs, vertical trunk
Side-shuffle · COM travel
  • The legs remain in a loaded athletic position and the trunk remains vertical.
1Athletic position
Side-shuffle · Posture
  • An athletic position is maintained throughout.
2Joint flexion
Side-shuffle · Posture
  • Maintain flexion of the ankles, knees and hips, lowering the COM.
3Flat back
Side-shuffle · Posture
  • The back remains flat.
4Head in line
Side-shuffle · Posture
  • The head is in line with the body.
1Short, rapid arm action
Side-shuffle · Arm action
  • Perform a short, rapid arm action in the sagittal plane.
Backpedaling: rearward locomotion with periods of double-limb support and one foot in contact with the ground between contralateral foot strikes. Backward running: rearward locomotion with single-leg support throughout foot–ground contact and both feet in the air between foot strikes.

Topic 05 — Agility Performance & COD Ability
Technical Guidelines and Coaching
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Large degrees of freedom
Technical guidelines and coaching
  • In comparison to sprinting, COD and agility have a large degree of freedom, due to the multitude of movements that occur during a COD.
2No single technique
Technical guidelines and coaching
  • Agility performance, as restricted or determined by opponents or other tactical restraints and scenarios, cannot be trained through the use of a single technique.
3Variability and flexible coordination
Technical guidelines and coaching
  • Evidence suggests we should create within- and between-skill variability and a flexible coordinative approach.
4The guidelines
Technical guidelines and coaching
  • Nevertheless, the following are some technical guidelines and coaching suggestions: visual focus, body position, leg action, arm action.
1Scan the environment and opponent
Visual focus
  • When changing direction in response to an opponent (either offensive or defensive), the athlete should visually scan the environment and opponent.
  • Focus on the shoulders, trunk and hip.
2Redirect attention
Visual focus
  • Following the anticipation of the event, unless deception is intended, the athlete should quickly redirect attention to a new area.
  • This helps lead the transition of the body.
1Control the trunk
Body position during braking and reacceleration
  • Control the trunk leading into the deceleration (decrease large amounts of trunk motion).
  • When decelerating, posterior trunk lean may assist in orienting the force vector posteriorly.
2Reorient trunk and hips
Body position during braking and reacceleration
  • Through the stance phase, reorient the trunk and hips toward the direction of intended travel.
  • This allows a more effective reacceleration, and reduces the redirection demands for a more effective position to produce force.
3Body lean
Body position during braking and reacceleration
  • Just as with acceleration mechanics, body lean is paramount in allowing proper force application through the ground.
  • Keep strong alignment of the ankle, knee and hip to the trunk and shoulders.
4Lower center of mass
Body position during braking and reacceleration
  • Enter and exit changes in direction with a lower center of mass.
  • This increases stability and enables a manipulation of the base of support relative to the center of mass.
1Tolerate eccentric braking loads
Leg action
  • Ensure the athlete can effectively dissipate or tolerate the eccentric braking loads through an effective range of motion at the hip, knee and ankle (i.e., co-triple flexion).
  • Avoid a stiff-legged braking style.
2Firm base of support
Leg action
  • Emphasize a firm base of support for effective push-off, and manipulation of the base of support relative to the center of mass.
  • Wide lateral foot plant when cutting; large anterior foot placement when turning.
3Push the ground away
Leg action
  • Push the ground away to enhance performance: rapid simultaneous triple extension of the ankle, knee and hip.
  • Especially important while learning in closed drills.
4External focus of attention
Leg action
  • Instructions to concentrate on the ground instead of a body part have been shown to improve COD performance.
1Powerful arm actions
Arm action
  • Powerful arm actions should be used to facilitate leg drive.
2Arms must not be counterproductive
Arm action
  • Ensure the action of the arms does not cause a decrease in speed or efficiency, particularly when transitioning between difficult COD (e.g., from a backpedal to a sprint).
  • Keep the arms close to the body to reduce the moment of inertia and increase the total body rotation velocities when changing direction.
1Three phases of agility
Transitional movements
  • Expressions of agility can be divided into three phases.
  • Transition: the athlete is in a ready position to read, and then react to, a situation that arises.
  • Initiation: the moment an athlete initiates or changes movement (e.g., a COD).
  • Actualization: a sport skill or sprint to a position.
2Example: corner back
Transitional movements
  • A corner back tracking a wide receiver may perform a backpedal (transition).
  • Then a directional change (initiation) into a sprint, and then intercept an underthrown pass (actualization).
3Earlier phases matter too
Transitional movements
  • The success of a play manifests in the actualization phase.
  • But the preceding phases are just as important and require good technical execution.
4Backpedaling
Transitional movements
  • Rearward locomotion with periods of double-limb support and one foot in contact with the ground between contralateral foot strikes.
5Backward running
Transitional movements
  • Rearward locomotion involving single-leg support throughout foot–ground contact, with both feet simultaneously in the air between foot strikes.
6Forward visual gaze
Transitional movements
  • Either may be performed to displace an athlete rearward while maintaining a forward visual gaze of an opponent or ball.
  • Examples: basketball, soccer, rugby and football.
7Sport dependent
Transitional movements
  • The frequency and importance of differing transitional movements may be sport dependent.
  • More research is required in specific sports to develop this understanding.
8Develop a variety
Transitional movements
  • Practitioners should develop their athletes' ability to perform a variety of transitional movements (e.g., lateral shuffle, backpedal, crossover running).
  • And to perform sprints from these transitional movements, to develop movement solutions and all-around physical literacy.

Topic 06 — Methods of Developing Agility
Methods of Developing Agility
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Multifactorial approach
Methods of developing agility
  • As discussed throughout the chapter, a multifactorial approach is warranted to develop both the physical and the perceptual-cognitive aspects required for continual improvement in agility performance.
2Strength strategies
Methods of developing agility
  • Address the underpinning physical capacities using various strength development strategies.
3Closed-skill COD technique
Methods of developing agility
  • Build technical competence in a closed-skill environment, with movement-specific actions (COD ability).
4Perceptual-cognitive capacity
Methods of developing agility
  • Improve perceptual-cognitive capacity through agility drills and the inherent aspects of skills practice.
1Same as speed, plus eccentric
Strength for agility
  • Similar to strength development for speed, emphasize relative strength and a variety of speed-strength qualities along the force–velocity spectrum.
2Extra eccentric strength
Strength for agility
  • Consider additional development of eccentric strength, because of the large braking forces during deceleration and COD actions within expressions of agility.
3Load–velocity profiles
Strength for agility
  • Training can include a spectrum of load–velocity profiles in the weight room.
  • In the field, use a variety of load–velocity profile activities (squat jumps, countermovement jumps, and drop jumps of various heights) in combination with the COD and agility drills themselves.
4Well-rounded approach
Strength for agility
  • The multifactorial nature of agility warrants a well-rounded approach to strength development that spans the load– and force–velocity curve.
  • Examples of how weight-room and field training can satisfy the strength requirements underlying agility are on the Strength for Agility slide.
5Gains lag behind
Strength for agility
  • Athletes develop the physical requirements before they can transfer newly gained strength into technical competence.
  • So performance gains will lag behind the fundamental physical requirements for a given technical skill.
1Progress like plyometrics
COD ability
  • Similar to plyometric progressions based on the intensity and difficulty of each drill, closed-skill COD drills can progress from beginner to intermediate to advanced.
2Based on physical loading
COD ability
  • Progress based on the physical loading demands discussed in this chapter: regulation of angle and intensity, which affect mechanical loading.
3Drill progressions
COD ability
  • An example progression of drills for COD ability (both rapid COD and those associated with maneuverability) is presented, as well as a progression plan for agility drills.
4Agility loads more
COD ability
  • The physical loading during agility drills will be higher than in beginner COD drills.
5A guideline for advancing
COD ability
  • The progression gives practitioners a series of drills and a guideline for safely and effectively advancing athletes, so they can build on their physical and technical attributes as they improve.
1Skills practice vs agility drills
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • During years of skills training (within the sport), athletes continually enhance visual scanning, pattern recognition and knowledge of the situation.
  • In drills used to improve agility (outside skills practice), they primarily improve anticipation, decision-making time and accuracy.
2Train it like a physical task
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • In the same way one regularly increases the demands of a physical task to improve performance, one can train perceptual-cognitive ability.
3Start from closed-skill COD drills
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • Agility activities should begin by adding a perceptual-cognitive component (progressing from low to high cognitive loading) to common closed-skill COD drills.
4Generic stimuli
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • Decelerations or the Z-drill can evolve into agility drills by adding a generic stimulus: a whistle, a voice command, or a flashing arrow or light.
5Sport-specific stimuli
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • Following success with those agility drills, progress to activities with sport-specific stimuli, such as evasive drills and small-sided games.
  • These are said to have better transfer to performance.
6Temporal and spatial stress
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • Both generic and specific stimuli can be made harder within a drill through progressive increases in temporal (time) or spatial (space or area) stress on the athlete.
7Agility drill factors
Perceptual-cognitive ability
  • A range of agility factors can be manipulated in agility drill design: mechanical and perceptual-cognitive (see the Agility Drill Factors slide).

Topic 06 — Methods of Developing Agility
Strength for Agility
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Required
Dynamic strength
  • Base strength for all subsequent training, as well as adequate mobility during body weight and loaded training.
2Novice · weight room
Dynamic strength
  • Body weight exercises
3Novice · field/court
Dynamic strength
  • Body awareness work such as leaning drills
4Advanced · weight room
Dynamic strength
  • Squat (and variations)
  • Pulls (and variations)
  • Split-leg and unilateral variations
5Advanced · field/court
Dynamic strength
  • Various COD drills
1Required
Concentric explosive strength
  • To effectively reaccelerate (propulsion) after the braking phase, or maintain a strong position through the transition phase of COD and agility. May include isometric strength work.
2Novice · weight room
Concentric explosive strength
  • Bilateral and unilateral box jumps
3Novice · field/court
Concentric explosive strength
  • Acceleration drills
  • Banded drills and isometric postural holds
4Advanced · weight room
Concentric explosive strength
  • Box jumps
  • Weightlifting-based exercises
  • Squat jumps (loaded)
  • Lower-limb ballistic exercises initiated from static positions
5Advanced · field/court
Concentric explosive strength
  • Advanced acceleration drills (e.g., sled push)
1Required
Eccentric strength
  • To develop the ability to effectively attenuate force, absorb energy, and support the large external lower-limb flexion moments required during the braking phase of COD and agility.
2Novice · weight room
Eccentric strength
  • Submaximal bilateral and unilateral landing stabilization exercises (drop landing, single-leg hop and hold)
  • Flywheel resistance training, lower-submaximal eccentrics, and tempo training
3Novice · field/court
Eccentric strength
  • Submaximal deceleration drills (forward emphasis and teaching various deceleration positions)
4Advanced · weight room
Eccentric strength
  • Advanced bilateral and unilateral landing stabilization exercises performed in various planes
  • Drop landings and receiving strength required during the catch phase of weightlifting-based exercises
  • Accentuated eccentric training
  • Maximal and supramaximal eccentrics and resisted eccentrics
5Advanced · field/court
Eccentric strength
  • Maximal deceleration drills (high velocity and various angles)
1Required
Reactive strength
  • To increase the ability to transfer from a high eccentric load to concentric explosiveness.
2Novice · weight room
Reactive strength
  • Drop landing and landing stabilization exercises
3Novice · field/court
Reactive strength
  • Beginner plyometrics (slow to fast SSC activities, bilateral to unilateral, sagittal to multiplanar)
4Advanced · weight room
Reactive strength
  • Loaded jumps
  • Drop jumps
  • Complex or contrast training
5Advanced · field/court
Reactive strength
  • Advanced plyometrics (fast SSC activities, unilateral, and multiplanar plyometrics)
1Required
Multidirectional strength
  • To hold body position strongly during a multitude of movement demands.
2Novice · weight room
Multidirectional strength
  • Lunges
  • Landmine skater squats
3Novice · field/court
Multidirectional strength
  • Low-velocity COD (e.g., Z-drill)
  • Lateral, backward, and forward COD drills
4Advanced · weight room
Multidirectional strength
  • Unilateral exercises
  • Greater degree of freedom exercises (e.g., landmine exercises)
5Advanced · field/court
Multidirectional strength
  • High-velocity COD drills
  • Challenging cutting-angle COD drills
1Required
Perceptual-cognitive abilities
  • To progress in visual scanning, effective anticipation, and decision making.
2Novice · field/court
Perceptual-cognitive abilities
  • Simple reaction drills: introduction to increasing either temporal or spatial uncertainty
3Advanced · field/court
Perceptual-cognitive abilities
  • Small-sided games
  • Agility drills with severely restricted temporal and spatial aspects
  • Virtual reality and video-based training

Topic 06 — Methods of Developing Agility
COD & Agility Drill Progressions
Point
Point
Point
1Beginner
COD
  • Deceleration drills (forward), progressing to higher entry velocity or shorter distance to stop.
  • Basic movement patterns for forward, backward and lateral shuffling.
  • COD drills involving low velocities (<5 yd [5 m] of acceleration into the COD), e.g., Z-drill.
2Intermediate
COD
  • Deceleration drills (lateral), with the same progressions as forward.
  • Expand to include a broad range of cutting angles less than 75°.
  • May increase entry velocity during drills (up to 10 yd [9 m] of acceleration leading into the COD).
3Advanced
COD
  • Deceleration to reacceleration in both forward and lateral directions.
  • Expand further to a comprehensive range of cutting angles, including those greater than 75°.
  • Maximal-effort decelerations and entry velocities.
1Beginner
Maneuverability
  • Basic drills or tests such as the Illinois agility, requiring nearly straight-line running with slight bends.
2Intermediate
Maneuverability
  • Drills that increase the difficulty of the bend involved, such as the L-run.
  • Drills that require transition between modes of movement (shuffling, sprinting and backpedaling), such as the T-test.
3Advanced
Maneuverability
  • Repeated maneuverability activities with manipulated work-to-rest ratios.
1Beginner
Agility
  • Physical and technical competence should come before agility drills are incorporated.
2Intermediate
Agility
  • COD drills from the beginner and intermediate categories, with the addition of simple stimuli (arrow, pointing in a certain direction).
  • These drills present a limited number of options to react to (e.g., right or left, forward or back) on the signal, so they do not develop agility per se.
  • However, they further increase the intensity of drills along the agility development continuum.
3Advanced
Agility
  • Expand into large degrees of spatial and temporal uncertainty (and therefore greater perceptual-cognitive stress).
  • Small-sided games.
  • Evasion games and drills.
Change-of-direction and agility drill progressions: beginner, intermediate, advanced.
