Topic 06 — Methods of Developing Agility
Agility Drill Factors
Point
Point
1Spacing and pitch or court dimensions
Mechanical factors
  • Altering the space and pitch or court dimensions varies the distances traveled, and so the entry and exit velocities and momentum achieved.
  • Athletes can develop agility from lower-velocity, intensive scenarios to higher-velocity, extensive scenarios.
2Entry and exit velocity (momentum)
Mechanical factors
  • Entry velocity regulates the intensity and the subsequent mechanical loading experienced.
3Agility actions and angle of COD
Mechanical factors
  • Restrict the type of COD action performed, or allow athletes to try a range of different COD actions, to develop between-skill variability and movement solutions.
  • Varying the location of end or target zones lets athletes develop shallow, moderate and sharp COD ability, to be proficient in changing direction across a spectrum of angles.
4Starting position (static or transitional movements)
Mechanical factors
  • Begin the drill from different static initiations (e.g., drop step, jab step) and from different transitional movements (backpedal, crossover running, lateral shuffle).
  • This creates drill variability, and increases game representativeness and the ability to evade or defend from different locomotor actions.
1Location and number of attackers or defenders
Perceptual-cognitive factors
  • The location of defenders and attackers can be manipulated: in addition to front-on situations, defenders can be located to the side or behind the attackers (pertinent for 360° sports).
  • Multiple attackers and defenders increase game representativeness: decoy runs; attacking and defensive transitions and set plays; team communication; and more chaos, task complexity, cognitive loading and variability.
2Temporal constraints
Perceptual-cognitive factors
  • Time constraints can be set (e.g., the athlete has 5 s to achieve the objective) to maintain quality and intensity, and often to replicate the reduced temporal constraints of random sports.
  • Work-to-rest ratios can be manipulated for energy system development and to represent peak demands of sports.
3Rules and conditions
Perceptual-cognitive factors
  • Practitioners can be creative and vary the rules (e.g., one-hand or two-hand tags).
  • They can put constraints on attackers or defenders to create variation (e.g., only two evasive actions can be performed before committing to a specific direction within the drill).
4Environment and surfaces
Perceptual-cognitive factors
  • To increase game representativeness, perform drills on the sport-specific surface.
  • Certain sports play on different surfaces (e.g., grass and artificial turf) with different hardness and frictional properties, which should be considered.
5Generic to sport-specific stimulus (representative learning environments)
Perceptual-cognitive factors
  • Generic stimuli and sources of information: auditory commands, generic visual commands, flashing lights, arrows, and coach- or player-dictated directional commands — these increase cognitive loading and mechanical loading in a controlled environment. The timing of stimuli can also be controlled using specific equipment.
  • To increase game representativeness, develop perceptual-cognitive speed, knowledge of situations, memory recall and anticipation, include sport-specific stimuli (multiple attackers or defenders, sport-specific implements and scenarios) to develop movement solutions and transfer to sporting performance.
  • These drills can be developed collaboratively with the skills coach, for simultaneous technical and tactical development.
6Task complexity and cognitive loading
Perceptual-cognitive factors
  • To challenge more advanced athletes and prepare them for the chaotic demands of sport when returning to sport, drills can begin with relatively simple closed and open drills with one or two stimuli and sources of information.
  • Then progress to more chaotic open drills of increased game representativeness, with various sources of stimuli and information (multiple attackers or defenders, sport-specific implements and stimuli).
Mechanical and perceptual-cognitive factors that can be manipulated during agility drills.

Topic 07 — Program Design for Speed
Program Design
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Several planning levels
Periodization
  • Program design involves planning at several levels, each with its own set of considerations.
  • Microcycles (short term), mesocycles (medium term) and macrocycles (long term).
2Periodization
Periodization
  • The process is referred to as periodization.
  • Periodization is the strategic manipulation of an athlete's preparedness through the employment of sequenced training phases defined by cycles and stages of workload.
3Fatigue and accommodation
Periodization
  • Planned workloads are varied to facilitate the integration of planned programming tactics.
  • These tactics harmonize the relationship between training-induced fatigue and accommodation.
4Guided by monitoring
Periodization
  • The periodization process is guided by information collected during the athlete monitoring process.
5Short- and long-term responses
Periodization
  • As an athlete progresses through a training phase, consistent information from various monitoring strategies shows how the athlete is responding to the training stimulus in the short term.
  • It also shows how the athlete should be further developed in the long term — that is, how the original training program should be modified to reflect responses to the training.
6Manipulating variables
Periodization
  • At each level of training plan development, strength and conditioning professionals must manipulate certain variables.
  • These are useful in characterizing the training agenda and quantifying workloads.
7Consider variables individually
Periodization
  • Each variable must be considered individually, and for how it affects the collective system.
  • Individual athlete training responses, revealed by athlete monitoring, should be used in the manipulation of these variables.
1Angle
Training variables · Movement variables
  • The intended angle for center of mass (COM) deflection during the task.
  • A regulator for knee joint loading.
2Approach velocity
Training variables · Movement variables
  • The horizontal entry velocity of the COM as the athlete begins to initiate their COD action over multiple steps.
  • A regulator for knee joint loading.
1Exercise (or work) interval
Training variables · Load variables
  • The duration or distance over which a repetition is executed.
2Intensity
Training variables · Load variables
  • The effort with which a repetition is executed (% of maximum).
3Volume
Training variables · Load variables
  • The amount of work (e.g., 3 sets of 5 repetitions) performed in a given training session or time period.
4Volume-load
Training variables · Load variables
  • The density of volume performed at prescribed intensities.
  • Example: 3 sets of 5 repetitions at 100 kilograms results in a volume-load of 1,500 kilograms.
5Work-to-rest ratio
Training variables · Load variables
  • The relative density of exercise and relief intervals in a set, expressed as a ratio.
1Exercise order
Training variables · Structure variables
  • The sequence in which a set of repetitions is executed.
2Frequency
Training variables · Structure variables
  • The number of training sessions performed in a given time period (e.g., day or week).
3Recovery (rest) interval
Training variables · Structure variables
  • The time period between repetitions and sets.
4Repetition
Training variables · Structure variables
  • The execution of a specific workload assignment or movement technique.
5Set
Training variables · Structure variables
  • A group of repetitions and rest intervals.
6Series
Training variables · Structure variables
  • A group of sets and recovery intervals.
1Resistance training periodization
Link to resistance training
  • The periodization of resistance training programs is explained separately.
2Same concepts apply
Link to resistance training
  • The same concepts can be applied to sprint, COD and agility training.

Topic 07 — Program Design for Speed
Speed Development Strategies
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Like weight-room planning
Planning for speed development
  • The planning process for speed development is similar to that used by strength and conditioning professionals in the weight room.
2Periodize physical and psychological components
Planning for speed development
  • Planning tactics should be periodized to address the physical and psychological components of sprinting.
  • Use emphasis and de-emphasis on particular qualities, in a phasic manner.
3Maximize and saturate a quality
Planning for speed development
  • An athlete's capability to sprint can be improved through training periods designed to fully maximize and saturate a fitness quality.
  • This may bolster the effects of future training agendas.
1Locomotion and force production
Force and neuromuscular factors
  • To enhance speed, a practitioner should consider the relationship between human locomotion and force production.
2Link to sprint success
Force and neuromuscular factors
  • Throughout the chapter, a link has been shown between sprint success and certain physiological phenomena.
3Elite sprinters
Force and neuromuscular factors
  • Elite sprinters produce large amounts of force within a short amount of time.
  • This high level of force allows the sprinter to produce longer step lengths at a faster rate.
4Neuromuscular factors
Force and neuromuscular factors
  • This display of movement on the track reflects enhanced neuromuscular factors: maximal strength, RFD and impulse.
5Product of well-designed training
Force and neuromuscular factors
  • These variables are the product of well-designed training protocols.
  • They aim to enhance qualities such as hypertrophy of task-specific motor units, firing frequency, rate coding and muscle–tendon stiffness.
1A phased option
Short-to-long model
  • An option for speed development is a set of sequenced training blocks (see the Speed Development Blocks slide).
  • Sequenced phases of training may seamlessly develop sprint potential through the maturation of accelerative abilities before the execution of maximal-velocity efforts.
2The short-to-long method
Short-to-long model
  • A conceptual progression that attempts to merge the relationship between larger rates of acceleration and greater sprint velocities (discussed earlier in the chapter).
3Start of the training year
Short-to-long model
  • The athlete begins the year emphasizing improved propulsive force output.
  • This is done through short sprints that maintain the biomechanics associated with the acceleration phase of a sprint.
4Later in the year
Short-to-long model
  • The athlete bridges into longer sprint work that aims to enhance top speed through upright running mechanics.
5The concept
Short-to-long model
  • An athlete may see greater improvements in top speed if force production can occur at the ideal rate and moment.
  • This comes through an investment in acceleration development and optimization.
1For 100–200 m track sprinters
Alternative approach for track sprinters
  • An alternative approach may involve sequencing training from general to specific preparation.
2Early phases
Alternative approach for track sprinters
  • Start with an aerobic foundation.
  • Then develop anaerobic capacity (short speed–endurance).
3Late phases
Alternative approach for track sprinters
  • Then speed–endurance (long speed–endurance).
  • Culminating in speed (inclusive of acceleration and maximum velocity) before the main competition.
Acceleration phase: braking impulse, then propulsive impulse
Maximal-velocity phase: much shorter ground contact
Acceleration phase: braking impulse, then propulsive impulse

Topic 07 — Program Design for Speed
Biomechanical Differences in Acceleration Between Sprint and Team-Sport Athletes
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Acceleration matters in both
Sprint vs team-sport acceleration
  • The ability to accelerate linearly and displace the COM rapidly is essential in track sprinting and in multidirectional team sports.
2Why study sprinters
Sprint vs team-sport acceleration
  • Track sprinters are the fastest humans on earth.
  • Examining the biomechanics and techniques they adopt is intuitive for understanding and optimizing sprinting performance in athletes.
3Clear differences exist
Sprint vs team-sport acceleration
  • Clear biomechanical and technical differences exist between sprint and team-sport athletes.
4Constraints interact
Sprint vs team-sport acceleration
  • Environment, task and performer constraints will all interact.
  • They influence the acceleration strategy and mechanics employed, and the overall execution of the sprinting skill.
1The study
Early acceleration (Wild and colleagues)
  • Wild and colleagues examined the first three steps during initial acceleration.
  • They compared sprinters with rugby forwards and backs.
2Sprinters: greater values
Early acceleration (Wild and colleagues)
  • Greater step velocities and greater normalized average horizontal external power.
  • Greater normalized step length and flight length.
  • Greater normalized touchdown distance (foot impact under or behind the COM) and greater toe-off distance (effective push-off behind the COM).
3Rugby backs
Early acceleration (Wild and colleagues)
  • Rugby backs displayed slightly shorter contact times and slightly greater step rates compared to sprinters.
1Matched velocities
Later acceleration (kinetics)
  • Compared at matched velocities: steps 8–12 for sprinters and steps 9–20 for soccer athletes.
2First 20% of stance
Later acceleration (kinetics)
  • No differences were observed between sprinters and soccer athletes in the initial 20% of the stance phase.
3Propulsive phase force
Later acceleration (kinetics)
  • Sprinters produced greater anterior–posterior force across most of the propulsive phase.
  • They also produced greater net forces over similar contact times, resulting in greater relative net impulse.
4Power and the velocity plateau
Later acceleration (kinetics)
  • Sprinters achieved greater average horizontal external power.
  • This allowed them to accelerate beyond the velocity plateau of the soccer athletes.
1Partial attribution
Why the differences · Sprinters
  • The observed spatiotemporal, kinematic and kinetic differences could be partially attributed to the factors below.
2Four-point start on blocks
Why the differences · Sprinters
  • Sprinters accelerate from a four-point position using blocks.
3Rubber surface and spikes
Why the differences · Sprinters
  • Sprinters perform on a rubber surface while wearing spikes.
4Body orientation
Why the differences · Sprinters
  • This results in different body segment orientations, such as greater forward trunk lean and horizontal shin angles.
  • These contribute to more horizontally oriented force.
5Sole task: linear speed
Why the differences · Sprinters
  • Sprinters' preparation strategies are designed around the sole task of maximizing linear speed, which is the aim of that sport, an isolated event.
6Skill and deliberate practice
Why the differences · Sprinters
  • Sprinting is a skill, so sprinters can dedicate more time and deliberate practice to developing it.
  • Their periodized strength and conditioning programs can also be tailored to maximize the physical qualities that underpin linear sprinting.
1Two-point staggered start
Why the differences · Team-sport athletes
  • Team-sport athletes initiate sprints from a more upright, two-point staggered-stance position.
  • This results in a more vertically oriented force.
2Surface
Why the differences · Team-sport athletes
  • A different surface, with less favorable frictional properties for achieving peak speed (grass, field turf, indoor courts).
3Footwear
Why the differences · Team-sport athletes
  • Footwear designed for multidirectional and sport-specific movements (e.g., cleats or trainers).
4Multidirectional movement
Why the differences · Team-sport athletes
  • Team-sport athletes must be proficient at a range of multidirectional movements: changing direction, curved sprints of varying radii and direction, and deceleration.
  • By comparison, sprinters perform curved sprints anticlockwise with radii ≥40 yd [36.5 m].
5Sport-specific skills and training
Why the differences · Team-sport athletes
  • They must also be proficient at sport-specific skills (e.g., passing, tackling, shooting).
  • They must perform technical and tactical training as well.
6Long matches and seasons
Why the differences · Team-sport athletes
  • And they generally must do so repeatedly over the course of long matches (generally 40–90 min) and competitive seasons.
7Less time on sprinting
Why the differences · Team-sport athletes
  • Because of these competing demands, team-sport athletes spend a significantly lower proportion of time developing sprinting skills.
  • Their preparation programs also differ, due to the different physical, biomechanical and cardiorespiratory fitness demands between sports.

Topic 07 — Program Design for Speed
Monitoring Sprint Ability
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Traditional testing
Monitoring sprint ability
  • The longstanding method of assessing speed is a test of maximal-effort linear sprinting.
  • It is usually carried out over a distance believed to be relevant to the athlete's sport, such as 40 yards (37 m).
2What time to completion misses
Monitoring sprint ability
  • Time to completion is an effective tool to evaluate changes in sprint performance.
  • But these tests do not fully address the minute changes in an athlete's progression toward race or field readiness.
3Testing error
Monitoring sprint ability
  • Testing error, in the form of hand timing and various start tactics, confounds the interpretation of results.
  • So strength and conditioning professionals may adopt additional monitoring tools as part of their battery of assessments.
4Cameras and optical timing
Monitoring sprint ability
  • High-speed cameras or optical timing systems that use interruptions of infrared light capture data from an athlete's collective foot strikes.
  • This gives additional insight into sprint capabilities, such as technique and movement strategies.
5Instantaneous speed
Monitoring sprint ability
  • Technology that quantifies instantaneous speed also gives insight into speed at specific distances, time to achieve specific speeds, peak speed, acceleration, and τ (acceleration time constant).
  • The key variables that may be useful in monitoring speed development are covered in the measure tabs.
1Description
Ground contact time
  • The total time allotted for a single stance phase.
2Interpretation
Ground contact time
  • In general, decreased ground contact times coupled with improved sprint completion times may suggest the athlete has improved the ability to generate high rates of force in a shorter amount of time.
  • However, an athlete may show slightly longer ground contact times at the initial stages of the sprint, due to acceleration mechanics.
1Description
Step length
  • The distance between the toe and heel of two consecutive footsteps.
  • Example: centimeters between the heel of the right foot and the heel of the left foot.
2Interpretation
Step length
  • Improvements in step length (increases in distance covered) may occur through improved sprint mechanics or posture, and ultimately enhanced force output.
1Description
Stride length
  • The distance between the heel in two consecutive steps of the same foot.
  • Example: meters between the heel of the right foot and the heel of the next ground contact made by the right foot.
2Interpretation
Stride length
  • Improvements in stride length (increases in distance covered by two successive steps) may occur through improved sprint mechanics or posture, and ultimately enhanced force output.
1Description
Flight time
  • The duration of time that an athlete is not in contact with the ground.
  • It occurs between the end of one step and the beginning of the subsequent step.
2Interpretation
Flight time
  • Increases in flight time can be interpreted in two ways:
  • (1) The athlete is producing higher vertical forces over a shorter amount of time, resulting in optimal horizontal displacement of the athlete's mass down the track.
  • (2) The athlete is producing higher forces over a longer amount of time, which may result in unnecessary vertical amplitude of the center of mass.
1Description
Stride angle
  • The angle at which the foot leaves the track.
2Interpretation
Stride angle
  • The stride angle may let the strength and conditioning professional determine whether the athlete is producing forces at the right moment, which is achieved through proper sprint mechanics.
  • Stride angle data also show what stage of sprint the athlete is in (acceleratory, transitory, maximum speed) and may relate to ground contact times.
1Description
Speed
  • The relationship between steps and the sum of the first step's ground contact time and the flight time leading to the subsequent ground contact.
  • Alternatively, instantaneous speed or velocity can be examined using GPS technology, LiDAR, laser, radar, motorized resistance devices, and 2D and 3D motion capture.
2Interpretation
Speed
  • Speed dictates how fast an athlete can move the body mass over a specific distance.
  • Instantaneous speed/velocity at time points or distances can be calculated, giving greater insight into sprint strategy.
1Description
Acceleration
  • The change in speed, as determined by the delta of two steps (e.g., right heel to left heel) and the sum of the ground contact times and flight times of each step.
2Interpretation
Acceleration
  • Acceleration shows how well the athlete changes speed (increasing velocity in a direction) over a prescribed distance.
  • For most athletes, increasing the length over which they can accelerate will lead to a higher top speed, provided that postural integrity and mechanics are sound.
1Description
Technique
  • Acceleration and maximum velocity techniques can be objectively quantified (e.g., joint angles) or qualitatively examined and compared to technical models.
  • This helps improve performance and mitigate injury risk.
2Interpretation
Technique
  • Qualitative analysis is relatively simple to perform and only requires filming of sprint technique.
  • High-speed video recording is a common feature of most smartphones and tablets.
  • Technique can be compared to technical models such as the Altis Kinogram or SprintMechanics assessment score, to help individualize training.
ETG = electronic timing gate; 2D = two-dimensional; 3D = three-dimensional; LiDAR = light detection and ranging.

Topic 08 — Program Design for Agility
Agility Development Strategies
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Periodized programming
Agility development approach
  • The development of agility is best achieved using a periodized programming method.
2Random or sport-specific only
Agility development approach
  • Random programming, or developing agility using only sport-specific methods such as small-sided games, has not been found to be as effective.
3Agility is always present
Agility development approach
  • Agility is a constant element on the field of play and during skills practices.
4Start with preplanned COD drills
Agility development approach
  • It is recommended that agility development begin with COD drills (preplanned).
  • Progress in difficulty through increases in the physical demands.
5Then add perceptual-cognitive stress
Agility development approach
  • This is followed by the addition of drills involving perceptual-cognitive stress — what are typically termed agility drills.
6Start with a needs analysis
Agility development approach
  • The development of agility should start with a needs analysis based on assessment of the athlete's COD ability and agility.
7The agility test
Agility development approach
  • The agility test should specifically evaluate perceptual-cognitive ability.
  • Depending on the additional movement requirements of the sport, one may also choose a test that is more dependent on maneuverability.
8Largest window of opportunity
Agility development approach
  • The following steps are an example of how to determine the appropriate tests, analyze the results, and use them to program agility development.
  • Because agility performance is underpinned by multiple factors, target the largest window of opportunity through direct assessment of the athlete's strengths and weaknesses.
1Step 1: Needs analysis
The five steps
  • Perform a needs analysis of the sport and match tests appropriately to assess these qualities.
2Step 2: Strengths and weaknesses
The five steps
  • Determine strengths and weaknesses by comparing results as a standardized score to performance standards or the team mean.
3Step 3: Primary and secondary need
The five steps
  • Plan the development of a primary area of need and a secondary area of need for the athlete.
4Step 4: Distribute the time
The five steps
  • Distribute the time available for this development based on need identification.
5Step 5: Plan the distribution and monitor
The five steps
  • Provide a preliminary plan for the transition of percent distribution through the training blocks.
  • Determine if this progression is appropriate by monitoring the development of COD and agility using measures such as the COD deficit.
1The example
Needs analysis example
  • Sport: basketball.
  • Timeframe: 12 weeks (8 weeks of off-season and 4 weeks of preseason training).
2High-velocity COD
Needs analysis example
  • Sport-specific agility needs analysis: backdoor cuts, cuts through the lane, fast breaks, and possession changes.
3Maneuverability
Needs analysis example
  • Multiple modes of COD movement.
  • Defensive shuffling, backpedaling, and bending changes of direction around screens to lose a defender.
4Agility (perceptual-cognitive)
Needs analysis example
  • Decision-making time, which provides great advantages both offensively and defensively.
  • The ability to move in reaction to play or an opponent.
5Recommended tests
Needs analysis example
  • The 5-0-5 including COD deficit, the T-test, and an agility test (decision time measured).
6Standardized scores
Needs analysis example
  • An athlete's strengths and weaknesses can be shown as standardized scores for perceptual-cognitive ability, maneuverability and COD ability.
  • Negative values indicate performance lower than average; positive values indicate performance better than average.
1What the plan shows
Planned distribution of training blocks
  • Planned distribution of training blocks for agility development.
  • COD is the primary aim, maneuverability the secondary aim, and agility (perceptual-cognitive) the tertiary aim.
  • Estimated percentage of time allotted through the blocks.
2COD (primary aim)
Planned distribution of training blocks
  • Block 1 ~65%; Block 2 ~60%; Block 3 ~50%.
  • Comment: check strength, or specifically load absorption ability, with drop landings.
3Maneuverability (secondary aim)
Planned distribution of training blocks
  • Block 1 ~35%; Block 2 ~30%; Block 3 ~25%.
  • Comment: assess body positioning during lateral shuffling and COD.
4Agility, perceptual-cognitive (tertiary aim)
Planned distribution of training blocks
  • Block 1 N/A; Block 2 ~20%; Block 3 ~25%.
  • Comment: may be reliant on perceptual-cognitive ability; this may have previously masked the identification that the athlete could improve his or her physical COD ability.
Topic 08 — Program Design for Agility

Agility Development Blocks

Three 4-week blocks · sessions of 10–15 min including work and rest, 1–3× per week · rest between sets in parentheses.
Block 1 · Linear deceleration capacity
PrimaryCOD (deceleration capacity — linear)SecondaryManeuverability (body position)Frequency2–3 sessions per week; rest period between sets
COD drill
Decelerations* (5 yd [5 m] start-stop)1 × 6 (30 s)
Alternate nonpreferred and preferred leg to finish the braking (split stance) position, and the bilateral athletic ready position.
Maneuverability drill
Lateral shuffling @ height or backpedaling1 × 4 × 11 yd [10 m] (30 s)
Training tools & notes
1Braking tasks are eccentric-focused → start with low volumes, similar to those used to introduce eccentric tasks (plyometrics).
2Focus on the athlete staying low, sacrificing speed for positioning, and emphasizing optimal deceleration mechanics.
* Speed should progressively increase for deceleration drills through the weeks — e.g., half speed to three-quarters speed entry velocity, or changing the distance of start-stop drills — including generic and sport-specific stimuli.
There is no separate emphasis on acceleration ability here; it is expected to be addressed alongside speed sessions.
Block 2 · Lateral deceleration capacity
PrimaryCOD (deceleration capacity — lateral)SecondaryManeuverability (transition between modes of COD — shuffle to sprint to shuffle)Frequency2–3 sessions per week; rest periods between sets
COD drill
Decelerations* (11 yd [10 m] start-stop)1 × 6 (30 s)
As in week 1; use the same variations.
Decelerations (lateral)1 × 4 (30 s)
Maneuverability drill
Z-drill (forward)2 × 4 (30 s; 2 min)
Always alternate start direction: left to right vs right to left.
Y-drill with different cutting maneuvers (side-step, crossover, split-step)3 × 4 (1 min; 3 min)
Develops movement solutions. Complete the exit from the directional change into a rapid deceleration. Generic stimuli can be added later within the block.
Training tools & notes
1Ensure the athlete can use body position to brake effectively when oriented both forward and laterally; focus on absorbing into the stop. Expand to a single effort in reaction to a generic stimulus.
2Promote effective force application into the ground ("pushing the ground away"); watch shank angle and trunk position for visual feedback.
* Speed should progressively increase for deceleration drills through the weeks — e.g., half speed to three-quarters speed entry velocity, or changing the distance of start-stop drills — including generic and sport-specific stimuli.
There is no separate emphasis on acceleration ability here; it is expected to be addressed alongside speed sessions.
Block 3 · Deceleration to reacceleration
PrimaryCOD (effective deceleration to reacceleration)SecondaryManeuverability (combine effective transition and body positioning)TertiaryAgility (keep COD performance and body position even in response to a generic stimulus)Frequency1–2 sessions per week (depending on skills volume); rest period between sets
COD drill
Modified 5-0-5 drill2 × 4 (30 s; 2 min)
Alternate plant foot.
Maneuverability drill
T-test1 × 4 (30 s)
Agility
Reactive agility (Y agility drill)1 × 4 (30 s)
Same direction in response to pointing in a direction.
Skills training
Also inherently contains sport-specific stimulus training.
Training tools & notes
1Focus on "braking in" and "exploding out" of the COD.
2Focus on footwork and staying low, with steps that promote a "drop and drive" out of the COD.
3Checks the transfer of physical training to a more specific (yet still generic stimulus) task. Focus on "decide and go": check athletes reorient and move as effectively as they decide.
There is no separate emphasis on acceleration ability here; it is expected to be addressed alongside speed sessions.

Topic 08 — Program Design for Agility
Monitoring Agility Development
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
Point
1Description
Completion time
  • The total time to complete the task.
2Interpretation
Completion time
  • Represents the duration it takes the athlete to get from A to B.
  • But it can be biased toward athletes with superior linear speed, and provides limited information regarding COD ability, technique or strategy.
  • Can be simply assessed using a stopwatch or ETGs.
1Description
COD deficit
  • The difference in time between a straight-line sprint and a COD test of equal length.
2Interpretation
COD deficit
  • Gives insight into the additional amount of time the athlete needs because of the demands of COD.
  • Example: subtract the 10 m sprint time from the 5-0-5 COD time (a common COD test is 10 m in length).
  • However, COD deficit can be biased toward slower athletes, and provides limited information regarding COD ability, technique or strategy.
1Description
Ground contact time
  • The total time the foot is in contact with the ground during the COD (the length of the plant phase: the main execution plant foot contact).
2Interpretation
Ground contact time
  • Shorter ground contact times are generally associated with faster COD performance.
  • They indicate the athlete is spending less time performing the COD (if the athlete deflects their COM at the same angle).
  • GCT can show whether the athlete is improving their COD ability irrespective of total time.
  • Measure it with a built-in force platform or contact mat, or verify it using 2D analysis.
1Description
Exit velocity
  • The horizontal velocity of the athlete during the initial step out of the plant of the COD.
  • Considered the first step of reacceleration, from plant foot to foot strike.
2Interpretation
Exit velocity
  • Unlike total time, using a high-speed video camera or 3D motion analysis to assess the athlete's velocity (at the hip or COM) gives a direct measure of the ability to change direction.
  • Improved exit velocity with the same or faster ground contact times implies greater RFD relevant to improving COD ability.
1Description
Entry velocity
  • The velocity of the athlete before the plant phase.
  • It can be measured over several steps, or as the last step entering the plant phase of the COD.
2Interpretation
Entry velocity
  • Entry velocity is a strong determinant of COD completion time, and the ability to enter the COD with high velocity can be advantageous for COD actions.
  • It can show whether any pacing or self-regulatory strategies are adopted.
  • Assessed using the same methods as exit velocity.
1Description
Decision-making time
  • The time between two events is considered decision-making time, and can be a positive or a negative value.
  • It can be broken into two orientations, to assess how athletes respond during game scenarios: (a) defensive (move in the same direction as the stimulus); (b) offensive (move in the opposite direction to the stimulus).
2Interpretation
Decision-making time
  • Similar to entry and exit velocity, a high-speed camera can be positioned to the side of the directional change to capture both the stimulus and the athlete's first definitive foot plant in response.
  • A negative decision-making time indicates the athlete anticipated the directional change before the stimulus finalized the movement.
  • Negative values are observed only in response to the movements of another person (video or human stimulus), highlighting the importance of stimulus specificity in agility protocols.
  • Measuring decision-making time in both defensive and offensive situations lets strength and conditioning professionals identify whether athletes need to develop perceptual-cognitive ability in a specific game scenario.
1Description
COD phase-specific information
  • Kinetic or kinematic data for the approach (or acceleration), deceleration, turn, and reacceleration phases of a COD task.
2Interpretation
COD phase-specific information
  • Lets the practitioner examine the overall COD by splitting the task into phases (e.g., approach, COD, and exit).
  • This identifies the COD strategy and establishes strengths and areas for development — essentially, how the athlete achieved that completion time.
  • Advanced technology such as LiDAR or radar may give information on braking time and distance, and speed at braking onset.
1Momentum into the COD
Alternative considerations
  • Consider the athlete's momentum into the COD task.
  • Greater momentums require greater braking impulse to decelerate.
2Pacing strategies
Alternative considerations
  • Additional monitoring of pacing strategies is also essential.
  • Athletes may regulate entry speed to reduce momentum, making deceleration or braking easier.
3Video analysis
Alternative considerations
  • Video analysis is also recommended, to observe technique.
  • It helps identify compensatory strategies, areas for development, and comparison to technical models.
COD = change of direction; COM = center of mass; ETG = electronic timing gate; 2D = two-dimensional; 3D = three-dimensional; LiDAR = light detection and ranging.
Topic 09

Speed &
Agility
Drills

Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 1: Ankling
  • PurposeDevelop the correct foot contact strategy for max-velocity sprinting.
  • StartTall stance; torso over hips, knees, ankles (stacked joints).
  • MovementPush off one limb through the ankle → small flight phase. Land on the forefoot under hips/COM, ankle neutral. Minimal knee + ankle flexion: "punch the ground" with short, stiff contacts.
  • Trunk + armsUpright, slight lean, hips extended. Contralateral arm small ROM, matching foot-contact rate.
  • TipsNo leaning back. Drive vertically on each contact. Avoid excess hip flexion (contact ahead of COM) → contact under COM.
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 2: A-Skip
  • PurposeDevelop leg recovery mechanics for max-velocity running.
  • StartTall stance, stacked joints. Lift one leg: thigh near parallel; swing foot at stance-knee height, heel under buttocks, ankle dorsiflexed ("figure four").
  • MovementDrive swing leg down through an active foot (slight dorsiflexion, big toe up) to near-triple extension of the new stance leg. Land fore-/mid-foot under hips. As contact begins, the opposite leg pops up to become the swing leg.
  • ResultActive push down + skipping motion → horizontal displacement down the track.
  • TipsTall posture, relaxed shoulders. Arms move at the same rate as legs, no pause between cycles.
  • Regress / progressA-march (slower; hands on hips if arm coordination struggles) → running form with thighs reaching parallel.
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 3: B-Skip
  • PurposeDevelop leg recovery + subsequent touchdown mechanics for max-velocity running.
  • StartTall stance, stacked joints. Same "figure four" swing-leg position as the A-skip (front-side mechanics).
  • Key differenceMore aggressive drive of the swing leg down → touchdown mechanics + higher angular velocities.
  • MovementDrive down through an active foot to near-triple extension; sweep the leg back to land fore-/mid-foot under hips. Opposite leg pops up on contact. Push-down force + skipping → horizontal displacement.
  • TipsTall posture, relaxed shoulders. Arms match leg rate. Hands on hips at first if arm coordination struggles.
  • Regress / progressB-march or B-walk → running form emphasizing leg recovery to touchdown; overhead variations for trunk stability + lumbopelvic control.
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 4: Switches
  • PurposeRapid limb switching; foot path resembling the linear path of accelerative sprinting.
  • StartStand on one leg; other leg flexed 90° at hip + knee (thigh parallel), ankle neutral/dorsiflexed (front-side mechanics, positive shin angle). Contralateral arm: elbow <90°, hand near chin height. Trunk upright, head up.
  • MovementDrive the standing leg up and the flexed leg down at the same time. Arm speed matches leg speed. Both land/flex together; pause in the start position, then repeat.
  • TipsUpright trunk + head; no leaning back or excess lumbar flexion. Rapid leg + arm switching; avoid thigh/knee lifts above 90°.
  • Progress2–3 reps on the spot before pausing → mini-hop forward between reps (rhythmic) → overhead variations.
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 5: Dribbles
  • PurposeScaled running practice emphasizing the circular foot path of max-velocity sprinting.
  • StartFeet hip-width; head + trunk upright.
  • MovementLift one foot above the opposing ankle, toes up; sweep down and back to contact. As COM moves ahead of the foot, the foot drives up and over the ankle. Repeat with each limb. Ankle neutral; may begin heel-to-toe.
  • Trunk + armsSlight forward lean, head up. Contralateral arm lower amplitude than sprinting; timing + ROM match the legs.
  • RegressWalking pace with heel-toe contact.
  • ProgressAnkle dribble → calf dribble → knee dribble → dribble bleeds (ankle → calf → knee in one rep, or knee dribble blended into a high-speed run). Contact progresses to forefoot.
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 6: Straight-Leg Bound
  • PurposeRapid retraction of the lower limb → touchdown mechanics of max-velocity sprinting; ↑ hip angular velocity + foot touchdown velocity.
  • StartFeet hip-width; head + trunk upright.
  • MovementUpward + forward hop from one limb. Keep the limb straight (extended knee, neutral ankle). Drive the opposite hip forward, then rapidly retract the limb to land on the forefoot before rebounding to the other limb.
  • TipsUpright, no leaning back. Rapid, forceful retraction. Short ground contacts, ideally under hips. Contralateral arm matches timing + ROM.
  • RegressReduce hip flexion ROM + retraction speed; build up gradually.
  • ProgressOverhead variations (trunk stability, lumbopelvic control) → blend into upright running, e.g., 20 yd straight-leg build-up into a flying 20 yd sprint.
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 7: Incline Sprint (Resisted)
  • PurposeResisted sprint for physical + technical gains in the acceleration phase. Alternative: weighted sleds.
  • SetupCrouched start: dominant leg forward, back leg 1–2 foot lengths behind. Split length = compromise between force generation vs lower center of gravity and comfort. Legs in line with pelvis (no hip twist).
  • PositionDrop the back knee straight down (shin near parallel to ground). Tall, rigid torso. Arm opposite the front leg near/above forehead, hand 6–8 in (15–20 cm) away. Rear arm back, hand by lateral buttock, elbow 100–120°. Lean forward until 60% of body weight is on the front leg; don't break at the waist.
  • MovementAggressive push down + through the ground via the front leg. Back leg assists but leaves earlier. Arms synchronous with legs.
  • TipsLow heel recovery of the rear leg. Keep pushing; hand pulled down and back. Torso tall + tight, head neutral and in line; torso rises at the same rate as the hips.
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 8: Deceleration Drill
  • PurposeReduce horizontal momentum (negative acceleration) over a series of foot contacts, alone or before a COD.
  • TaskAccelerate linearly from a two-point static start over a set distance (5, 10, or 20 yd/m), then brake over a series of steps as fast as possible.
  • ProgressStart submaximal, preplanned, short approach → ↑ intent, distance, velocity, momentum. Add stimuli: "Stop at the Lights" (green = accelerate, red = decelerate; DQ if you can't stop), auditory ("stop"), partner or opponent.
  • Start variationsTwo-point, three-point, falling, false step, amplitude jump, crossover cut, pivot, torso rotation, drop step, pop steps.
  • Deceleration positionsBilateral (athletic ready), split, transverse (jockey), lateral, diagonal (crossover).
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 9: Y Agility Drill
  • PurposePlant the foot laterally opposite the direction of travel → propulsive impulse into the new direction. Cutting is the key movement.
  • TaskAccelerate linearly from a two-point static start (e.g., 5 yd/m), side-step cut 45° left or right, accelerate another 5 yd/m.
  • ProgressSubmaximal, preplanned, short approach → maximal or longer approach (↑ approach velocity + momentum → ↑ braking demand). Add generic stimuli (color cone, left/right command), then sport-specific (opponent; mirror drills alternating attack + defense).
  • Crossover cutPlant foot on the same side as the new direction (or medially across the pelvic midline); cross the opposite leg in front; accelerate in the direction of the push-off leg.
  • Split step cutSmall amplitude jump before push-off, land with feet ≥ shoulder-width apart; the contralateral limb pushes off into the new direction.
Setup for the multiplanar acceleration initiation box drill
Progressions: (a) generic stimuli, (b) sport-specific stimuli
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 10: Multiplanar Acceleration Initiation Box
  • PurposeStart movements that accelerate the athlete in a new direction: forward, sideways, rearward.
  • TaskStart in the center of a 5 × 5 yd/m box. Accelerate from a static position in a new direction, then decelerate at the cone or zone. Begin submaximally.
  • Forward startsBilateral to false step, two-point staggered, three-point stance, prone, kneeling, supine, two-point staggered with torso rotation.
  • Sideways startsJab step (side-step cut), split step (amplitude jump), shuffle step, crossover or pivot, kneeling, two-point staggered with torso rotation.
  • Rearward startsPivot, drop or pop turn, turns from nondominant + dominant sides.
  • ProgressGeneric stimulus (color cone or command: left, right, forward, rear left, rear right) → sport-specific (opponent; mirror drills where the defender copies the initiation + direction).
Topic 09 — Speed & Agility Drills
Drill 11: Evasion Drill
  • PurposeOpen drill in a 10 × 10 yd/m box (e.g., 1v1 with two gates).
  • AttackerCreate + take space, create separation, evade, penetrate defensive lines accurately and efficiently into a specific end zone. Use COD, deceleration, linear, or curvilinear speed actions.
  • DefenderStop the attacker entering end zones, limit space, tag or delay. Read kinematic + postural cues, anticipate and react.
  • ProgressManipulate mechanical + perceptual-cognitive factors: larger pitch → ↑ entry/exit velocity + momentum, varied end zones. Add static mannequins or defenders for chaos. Use 2v2 small-sided games for transitions, organization, communication.
  • Variations1v1 with three gates; 1v1 with static defenders; 2v2 with static defenders.
